chapters.title: Start
chapters.hook: The sprint board can be full while the business is still standing in the dark.
chapters.counterintuition: Fast building is not proof, but motion tied to evidence can reduce a real question about customers, demand, or viability.
chapters.tryThisNow: Open one current project and write the single uncertainty your next build must answer. Then name the measurement that would change the following decision.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Treat startup work as managed learning: build only what can expose an assumption, measure the response, and let the next move change.

breakdown.fastRead:
Beth closes the grocery pilot board on Friday with every task checked off. The order sheets were printed. The display was stocked. The staff script was practiced. Yet nobody in the room can say whether customers wanted the seasonal box or only liked seeing it near the entrance.

That is the first correction: progress is not the amount of work finished. Progress is uncertainty reduced.

A startup is a group trying to make something new while key facts are unknown. That calls for more care, not less. If a team builds without checking behavior, it may only get better at hiding the truth. The loop matters because it ties motion to evidence.
breakdown.deepRead:
James has a stack of permit forms beside an empty tablet stand at city hall. The team can build the whole portal, celebrate the launch, and discover afterward that residents still call the desk for help. Or it can build one permit path first and watch whether people finish without picking up the phone.

The second choice looks smaller. It is actually more serious.

The Build-measure-learn loop earns its keep only when the next build is changed by what the last measure exposed. Build gives the uncertainty a shape. Measure lets the world answer. Learn means the answer changes the next decision, not merely the slide at the review.

Eric Ries puts management back into the startup room because uncertainty still has to be steered. Lean manufacturing enters here as more than a factory metaphor. In a factory, waste is visible when parts pile up before anyone knows whether they are right. In startup work, the pile may be features, meetings, polished designs, or a launch plan. The waste is not effort itself. The waste is effort placed too far from feedback.

You can move quickly and still be careful. The question is whether speed shortens the distance between assumption and evidence, or only multiplies activity. A team that builds one clean test may look slower than a team that ships six features. It may also be the only team learning how to build a sustainable business.
breakdown.fullRead:
Camille's bookkeeping app looks better every Saturday. The menu is cleaner, the invoice view is smoother, and the reminder email now has the right tone. Her laptop shows a crowded roadmap board, but the retention note at the bottom has stayed untouched for three weeks: will freelancers come back every Friday without being chased?

She deletes four cards. She keeps one test. Ten trial accounts will get the weekly reminder on Thursday, and the only result that matters by Monday is whether they return to reconcile receipts.

This is the difference between output and learning. Output can be counted as soon as the work is finished. Learning has to survive contact with the customer. It asks whether the business became less uncertain. If the answer is no, the work may still be beautiful, useful, or technically impressive. It just has not yet earned the right to be called progress.

What would make your current project less uncertain by Friday?

That question changes the shape of management. It pushes the team away from output theater, where the board is full and the story sounds strong, and toward continuous innovation, where each round of building is connected to a specific bet. The build-measure-learn loop is the steering wheel, not a slogan on the wall. The build is aimed at an assumption. The measurement is chosen before the team gets attached to the result. The learning tells the team whether to keep going, change the offer, narrow the customer, or stop protecting a bad idea.

Daniel sees the same issue on a hospital discharge project. Nurses have finished three new pamphlet drafts, each more polished than the last. The patient callback list still shows confusion about the first night at home. He turns the review away from pages completed and toward one question: which version reduces the call that starts with, I do not know what to do now?

The objection is easy to hear. Teams still have to build. Customers do not respond to theories. True. But building is not the disputed part. The dispute is whether the building is close enough to feedback to teach anything. A large release can bury the key lesson under too many moving parts. A smaller test can make one assumption answerable.

Starting well is not a burst of founder energy. It is a disciplined choice about what the next piece of work is supposed to reveal. A team under uncertainty does not need less management. It needs management that respects uncertainty enough to expose it.

Speed is useful only when it brings the truth closer.

Beth faces the same rule at the grocery pilot after the first Friday line clears. The staff script worked, the display looked full, and the preorder forms were neat. None of that answers whether customers want the seasonal box enough to repeat the purchase. The next loop has to measure that repeat behavior before the team adds more box options.

examples.title: Beth Puts the Pickup Log Beside the Preorder Sheet

planSpec.stakes: a seasonal rollout could burn shelf space on an untested demand signal
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sarah places one preorder page beside yesterday's pickup log and asks which assumption the next build should test

examples.scenario: At 7:20 a.m. Monday, Beth stands under the stockroom lights with a folded produce preorder sheet in one hand and yesterday's pickup log in the other. The pilot has a three-store cap, and the ops group wants to add two more seasonal boxes before launch. She places the preorder page beside the log and has to decide whether to approve the next build or ask which demand assumption the team is testing first. The pickup log must answer repeat demand before the team adds another seasonal box.
examples.whatToDo: Pause the rollout and make the next build answer one demand question. Use the pickup log to choose what evidence would prove customers want the seasonal box.
examples.whyItMatters: The team can fill shelves and still learn nothing. Pairing the preorder sheet with actual pickup behavior forces the work to reduce uncertainty before it expands.

examples.title: James Narrows the Permit Portal to One Path

planSpec.stakes: residents may still call the desk after a costly portal launch
planSpec.requiredBeat: James points to one permit type and asks the team to build only enough to see if applicants can finish without calling

examples.scenario: "Which permit creates the most calls?" James asks in the city hall conference room, tapping the stack of paper forms beside an empty tablet kiosk. The vendor wants a full portal scope by Friday. The call log says fence permits jam the desk every morning. James points to that form and must decide whether to fund the full build or test one path where residents finish without calling. The call log makes the uncertainty concrete because one permit path can show whether residents finish alone.
examples.whatToDo: Build the fence-permit path only far enough to test completion without phone help. Let the call log define whether the prototype taught the team anything.
examples.whyItMatters: The portal is not progress if residents still need the same desk call. A narrow path gives the uncertainty a clean answer before the city buys the larger system.

examples.title: Camille Deletes Four Roadmap Cards

planSpec.stakes: three months of polish may hide that freelancers will not return weekly
planSpec.requiredBeat: Camille deletes four roadmap cards and keeps only the retention question for Friday's test

examples.scenario: The laptop fan hums while Camille studies a crowded roadmap board for her freelance bookkeeping app. Trial accounts exist, the weekly reminder email is drafted, and every new card promises a nicer product. Her cursor hovers over four polish tasks. She must decide whether to keep improving the interface or delete the cards and run Friday's retention test. The retention note is the business question hiding under the cleaner invoice screen.
examples.whatToDo: Delete the polish cards and keep the weekly return test. Send the reminder email to trial accounts and judge progress by who comes back to reconcile receipts.
examples.whyItMatters: More polish can protect the project from the question that matters. Retention behavior tells Camille whether she is building a sustainable habit or a prettier silence.

examples.title: Daniel Changes the Discharge Review Question

planSpec.stakes: readmission work may produce prettier pamphlets without patient understanding
planSpec.requiredBeat: Daniel turns the sprint review from pages completed to which patient confusion was reduced

examples.scenario: You are beside Daniel at the nurse station, where a discharge folder with colored tabs sits beside the patient callback list. The quality-improvement team is proud of three finished drafts and a one question checklist. Before the review starts, Daniel has to decide whether to praise pages completed or ask which patient confusion actually went down. The callback list keeps the review tied to patient confusion rather than draft count.
examples.whatToDo: Move the review from completed pages to callback evidence. Ask which instruction reduced one repeated patient question, then build the next draft around that answer.
examples.whyItMatters: A better folder is only output until patient confusion changes. The callback list keeps the redesign tied to learning instead of decorative completion.

examples.title: Sophie Reads the Meal Credit Postmortem

planSpec.stakes: demo-day enthusiasm may not prove repeat use
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sophie watches signups pile up and asks what will show whether students come back next week

examples.scenario: It took Sophie until the Friday postmortem to see what the cafeteria table had hidden. On demo day, signup stickers filled the laptop lid, the meal credit code was scanned eighty times, and the team cheered. The return-date card beside the tray showed only six students came back. Sophie writes the rule for the next test: attention is not learning unless return behavior answers. The return-date card gives Sophie the behavior signal that demo-day attention could not provide.
examples.whatToDo: Separate first-day enthusiasm from repeat use. Keep the meal credit code, but make the next build depend on who comes back on the return date.
examples.whyItMatters: A busy demo table can flatter the team while leaving the business question untouched. Return behavior shows whether the marketplace is becoming useful after curiosity fades.

examples.title: Guillaume Circles One Repair Tag

planSpec.stakes: adding services may increase activity without proving a sustainable business
planSpec.requiredBeat: Guillaume circles the repair type that can reveal whether customers return before buying new tools

examples.scenario: The wall pegboard at Guillaume's hardware shop is half-filled with repair tags by Thursday afternoon. Before, he added every service customers mentioned and watched the cash drawer tally rise unevenly. After checking the repeat-customer list, he circles mower blade sharpening because it can reveal whether people return before buying new tools. The next week gets one test, not five new services. The repeat-customer list turns the repair menu into one learning cycle instead of a bundle of guesses.
examples.whatToDo: Choose the repair type that can prove repeat demand, then cap the next week around that test. Track whether customers return instead of counting service variety.
examples.whyItMatters: More services can make the shop busier without making the business clearer. One repeatable repair shows whether the work is building a sustainable pattern.

questions.prompt: A product team finishes six onboarding improvements in two weeks, but nobody can say whether new users are more likely to return after day three. What is the best reading of their progress?
choices: They have activity, but not yet validated progress unless the work reduced the retention uncertainty.
They have made clear progress because faster output creates more chances for success.
They should stop building until every customer question has been researched.
questions.explanation: The useful test is whether the sprint changed what the team knows about retention. Speed alone is the tempting wrong signal, while stopping all building avoids the learning loop.

questions.prompt: An operations lead has budget for a full scheduling tool, but the biggest unknown is whether technicians will update jobs from their phones. Which action best fits the starting move?
choices: Approve the full tool so technicians see the complete future workflow.
Build a small phone update test and measure whether technicians use it during one route.
Interview managers about why field updates usually fail.
questions.explanation: A small phone update test exposes the key uncertainty through behavior. A full tool hides the question under cost, and manager interviews may inform the test without replacing it.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit launches a polished volunteer portal and celebrates a thousand visits, but signups for actual shifts stay flat. What should the team ask first?
choices: Which color and copy changes would make the portal look more trustworthy?
How can the team drive more traffic to reach a bigger sample?
What did the launch teach about the assumption that visitors would commit to a shift?
questions.explanation: The core issue is whether visits turned into commitment, which tests the original belief. More traffic and surface polish may help later, but both can preserve output theater.

questions.prompt: A founder wants to add invoicing, time tracking, and tax reminders before testing her freelancer app. Her adviser insists on one weekly-return test first. Why is the adviser right?
choices: The weekly-return test tells whether the app is becoming a habit before extra features multiply the work.
A smaller feature list is always more attractive to customers.
Tax reminders are too complex for an early product.
questions.explanation: The return test measures a business uncertainty before the roadmap grows. The issue is not that fewer features are always better or that tax reminders are impossible.

questions.prompt: A city team tracks completed design tasks for a resident service, yet the help-desk call log has not changed. Which next metric would best restore the build-measure-learn loop?
choices: The number of interface screens finished by the vendor this month.
The percentage of residents who complete one service request without calling the desk.
The number of staff members trained on the new service language.
questions.explanation: Completion without a desk call measures whether the build answered the service uncertainty. Finished screens and staff training are outputs unless they change resident behavior.

questions.prompt: A team says, We learned customers love the product, after three friendly pilot users praise a demo but none return the next week. What is the flaw in that claim?
choices: The pilot group was too small for any discussion.
The team should have ignored qualitative feedback entirely.
Friendly praise was treated as learning before behavior validated the conclusion.
questions.explanation: The team promoted encouragement into proof without a behavior signal. Small samples can still teach, and qualitative feedback can help, but neither excuses the missing return evidence.

questions.prompt: A hardware shop owner adds knife sharpening, tool rental, and mower repair in the same week, then cannot tell why revenue rose. What did the large build damage?
choices: It mixed too many changes to show which service reduced uncertainty about repeat demand.
It made the shop look unfocused to regular customers.
It delayed hiring because each service needed different staff skills.
questions.explanation: The problem is not only brand focus or staffing. By changing too much at once, the owner lost the clean signal that would teach which service might support the business.

questions.prompt: A hospital team finishes a new discharge packet and gets praise from nurses, but patient callbacks still start with confusion about the first night home. What should leadership conclude?
choices: The packet has succeeded because nurses are the delivery experts.
The packet is not progress yet because the patient uncertainty has not moved.
The team should abandon discharge redesign and focus on readmission penalties.
questions.explanation: Patient confusion is the uncertainty the work needed to reduce. Nurse praise may matter for delivery, but it does not replace the behavior signal from callbacks.

questions.prompt: A team can either ship a complete beta in eight weeks or run a rough one-feature test next week that directly checks whether customers will pay. Which option better matches the opening discipline?
choices: Ship the complete beta because customers need the full picture before judging value.
Delay both options until the team has a confident annual roadmap.
Run the rough test because it brings the core business uncertainty into contact with evidence sooner.
questions.explanation: The rough test wins because it makes the key payment assumption answerable now. A complete beta may bury that signal, and a roadmap adds confidence without evidence.

reviewCards.front: A team shipped three features and still does not know whether customers return. What question restores progress?
reviewCards.back: Ask what uncertainty the work reduced. If no customer or viability question became clearer, the team has output, not validated progress. The next build should be aimed at one assumption the world can answer.

reviewCards.front: You see a roadmap packed with tasks under extreme uncertainty. What should you look for first?
reviewCards.back: Look for the build-measure-learn loop. Each task should connect to an assumption, a measurement, and a decision that could change afterward. If that chain is missing, the roadmap may be output theater.

reviewCards.front: A small test looks less impressive than a big launch. When is the small test the stronger start?
reviewCards.back: It is stronger when it answers the key customer or business uncertainty sooner. The size of the work matters less than whether feedback is close enough to steer the next move.

reviewCards.front: A manager wants to praise a busy team. What evidence should she ask for before calling the sprint progress?
reviewCards.back: She should ask what the sprint proved about customers, demand, or viability. Activity deserves credit, but startup progress means the business became less uncertain in a way that affects what happens next.

reviewCards.front: Why can fast building increase waste instead of reducing it?
reviewCards.back: Fast building increases waste when it pushes more effort through untested assumptions. Speed helps only when it shortens the path between assumption, measurement, and learning.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to turn visible work into managed learning. The skill is naming the uncertainty before the build, choosing the measurement before attachment sets in, and letting the result change the next decision.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a roadmap item does not name the customer uncertainty it will reduce, then rewrite it as a test or remove it from the next cycle.
If a sprint review starts with tasks completed, then ask what changed in customer behavior, demand, or viability because of those tasks.
If you are about to polish a feature for the third time, then choose one behavior signal that would prove whether the feature matters.
If a pilot is expanding because it feels busy, then cap the next version until one measurement shows what the first version taught.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one active project tomorrow and write the sentence, This build is meant to learn whether. Fill in one customer or viability uncertainty and one measurement that would change the next move.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Friday, review one piece of finished work and label it output, learning, or both. For anything labeled only output, decide what measurement would have made the work steerable.

memorableLines.text: That is the first correction: progress is not the amount of work finished.
memorableLines.why: It replaces the usual output scorecard with the chapter's central standard in one blunt sentence.

memorableLines.text: The second choice looks smaller. It is actually more serious.
memorableLines.why: The contrast makes a narrow test feel more disciplined than a large build.

memorableLines.text: Speed is useful only when it brings the truth closer.
memorableLines.why: It keeps the chapter from being misread as generic startup speed advice.

chapters.title: Define
chapters.hook: A badge from a giant company can still open the door to startup work.
chapters.counterintuition: The organization's costume is not the test, but unsettled facts define startup territory even inside budgets, policies, and legal review.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one project name, then mark the key facts as known or unknown: user, value, channel, repeat behavior, and funding model. Manage by the unknowns.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Define the work by uncertainty, not image; when the facts are unsettled, validated learning becomes the right progress measure.

breakdown.fastRead:
Anna walks into the glass conference room with a claims script on the screen. The company is old, regulated, and full of reporting lines. Still, the chatbot project has no clear answer to whether customers will trust it with a denied claim.

That is startup work when the key facts are still unsettled.

Size does not settle the question. Funding does not settle it. A logo on the wall does not settle it. The useful test is whether the team is creating something new while the important facts are still unknown. Once the work is uncertain, the scorecard should ask which facts became less unknown.
breakdown.deepRead:
"Entrepreneurs are everywhere" is not a compliment. It is a diagnostic. The sharper test is not whether someone looks entrepreneurial, but whether the facts around the work are still unsettled. A county library, a hospital unit, a large carrier, or a food bank can all be doing startup work if they are creating something new before demand, value, or usage has been proved.

That definition is stricter than the familiar image.

Ben sees it at the library returns desk. The building is stable. The patrons have cards. The tablet stand looks like a normal service upgrade. But nobody knows whether older patrons will borrow digital titles without staff help. If the team manages the pilot like routine service delivery, it will reward smoothness before it has earned understanding.

Stable environments can use stable management. Uncertain work needs a different fit. It still needs schedules, roles, and accountability. It also needs permission to expose assumptions without being punished for not already knowing the answer. Validated learning becomes the progress metric because ordinary execution metrics can look strong while the central unknown remains untouched.

The label matters because it changes what good management means.
breakdown.fullRead:
Celine stands in the food-bank warehouse with a route map pinned over crates of canned tomatoes. Donors want a fixed expansion plan by the end of the month. The two-depot limit is known. The truck capacity is known. What is not known is whether volunteers will adopt the new routing tool during a busy distribution week.

She draws a line down the wall. Known logistics on the left. Unknown volunteer adoption on the right.

That line is the real definition. Startup work is not a young-company costume. It is the condition of trying to create something new when the basic facts have not settled. A small bakery can be doing routine work. A government office can be facing startup uncertainty. A nonprofit can have decades of trust and still be guessing about a new service model. The outside shape tells you less than the inside unknowns.

Ask a harsher question: what would break if we managed this like the answers were already known?

Andrew faces that question in a medical device compliance group. The procedure binder is thick, and the company knows how to satisfy regulators. The blank ward map beside it tells a different story. Clinicians may not value the workflow enough to change their rounds. Andrew marks the compliance tasks as execution and the ward-adoption question as uncertainty. The same project now contains two kinds of work, and each needs a different scorecard.

This distinction prevents two mistakes. The first is romantic looseness, where people hear startup and assume discipline can relax. That is wrong. Uncertainty needs discipline because guesses are expensive. The second is institutional blindness, where a mature organization assumes all work inside it deserves mature-process standards. That is also wrong. A new service can suffocate when it is graded only on predictability before it has discovered what users need.

Validated learning keeps the definition honest in practice. If the facts are unsettled, progress means evidence that reduces those unknowns. A clean procurement timeline, a finished policy draft, or a polished claims script may still matter. It just cannot be the whole score. The team has to ask what the work proved about user behavior, value, adoption, or viability.

Hanna learns this after a school district attendance app review. The projector showed procurement dates, vendor milestones, and launch tasks. The room looked professional. Then she stopped the agenda and asked what nobody knew about parent use. The silence was the diagnosis. The work had been dressed like procurement while behaving like discovery.

Define the condition correctly, and the next move becomes clearer. Known work deserves execution management. Unknown work deserves learning management. Many projects contain both. The hard part is refusing to let the respectable parts hide the uncertain ones.

The badge on the door is not the test. The unknowns are.

examples.title: Anna Relabels the Claims Chatbot Review

planSpec.domain: insurance claims chatbot inside a large carrier
planSpec.stakes: routine delivery metrics could punish discovery work
planSpec.requiredBeat: Anna relabels the project from rollout to uncertainty map before the steering review

examples.scenario: At 8:10 a.m. Tuesday, Anna sits in a glass conference room with the claims script on the screen and the risk register open beside it. The steering review calls the chatbot a rollout, but the team still does not know whether customers will trust it after a denial. Before the executives arrive, Anna must decide whether to report delivery progress or relabel the work as an uncertainty map with a tight pilot boundary. The risk register makes the trust question visible before the chatbot is treated like routine delivery.
examples.whatToDo: Rename the work before the review. Separate known delivery tasks from unknown trust questions, then ask for a pilot boundary that lets the team learn without pretending the facts are settled.
examples.whyItMatters: A large carrier can still face startup uncertainty. If Anna lets routine delivery metrics define the project, the team may be punished for discovery work it actually needs.

examples.title: Ben Questions the Digital Lending Pilot

planSpec.stakes: a stable institution may hide unsettled user behavior
planSpec.requiredBeat: Ben asks whether patrons have a known problem or whether the team is still discovering it

examples.scenario: "Are we fixing a known problem, or still discovering one?" Ben asks beside the returns cart and the tablet checkout stand. Library cards are stacked for Saturday's pilot, and the patron notes disagree about what people need. The director wants a smooth launch plan. Ben must choose between treating the pilot as routine service work and naming the user behavior still unknown. The patron notes force Ben to separate a known desk process from an unknown borrowing behavior.
examples.whatToDo: Ask the room to classify the work before planning the launch. If patron behavior is still unknown, make the pilot measure that uncertainty instead of only checking service smoothness.
examples.whyItMatters: The library looks stable, but the digital lending behavior is unsettled. The right management fit depends on that condition, not on the age of the institution.

examples.title: Celine Splits the Food-Bank Wall

planSpec.stakes: donor pressure could force fixed plans before demand patterns are understood
planSpec.requiredBeat: Celine separates known logistics from unknown volunteer adoption on the wall

examples.scenario: The warehouse map curls at the corners above crates of canned tomatoes while Celine holds the volunteer signup sheet. Donors want a fixed routing plan, and the two depot limit is already known. The open question is adoption on distribution days. She must decide whether to send a confident plan or split the wall into known logistics and unknown volunteer behavior. The wall split protects the routing team from confusing truck facts with volunteer adoption.
examples.whatToDo: Draw the known and unknown columns before committing to the donor plan. Treat route capacity as execution and volunteer adoption as startup uncertainty that needs a test.
examples.whyItMatters: Pressure for a fixed plan can make uncertain work look settled. Celine protects the food bank from managing discovery as if it were ordinary logistics.

examples.title: Andrew Marks the Ward Map

planSpec.stakes: process discipline might mask that clinicians do not yet value the workflow
planSpec.requiredBeat: Andrew marks which parts are compliance execution and which parts are startup uncertainty

examples.scenario: You are in a regulated-company meeting with Andrew, a procedure binder open beside a blank ward map. The clinician interview notes are thin, but the compliance checklist is already detailed. Before the team locks the project plan, Andrew's pen hovers over two labels: execution for the known compliance work, uncertainty for the parts clinicians have not yet valued. The ward map keeps the unknown clinician behavior from hiding behind the thick compliance binder.
examples.whatToDo: Mark the compliance tasks separately from the clinician-adoption questions. Keep the regulated work disciplined while giving the uncertain workflow a learning metric.
examples.whyItMatters: Process strength can hide the part nobody knows yet. Andrew keeps compliance from becoming a costume that covers the real adoption risk.

examples.title: Hanna Stops the Attendance Agenda

planSpec.stakes: the project may be managed like procurement when family behavior is unknown
planSpec.requiredBeat: Hanna stops the agenda until the room names what no one knows about parent use

examples.scenario: It took Hanna one failed pilot to notice the projector had told the wrong story. The procurement timeline looked clean, the attendance letters were approved, and the parent SMS draft had a vendor date. The pilot school list still gave no answer on family use. In the postmortem, Hanna stops the agenda until the room names what no one knows about parents. The pilot school list shows that procurement polish did not answer the family-use question.
examples.whatToDo: Restart the review around unknown parent behavior. Keep procurement milestones, but do not let them stand in for evidence that families will actually use the app.
examples.whyItMatters: A school district can manage the purchase perfectly and still fail the discovery problem. Hanna changes the scorecard before the next pilot repeats the error.

examples.title: Luca Replaces the Membership Launch Checklist

planSpec.stakes: a respected brand may still be guessing about why visitors return
planSpec.requiredBeat: Luca replaces the launch checklist with an uncertainty checklist for repeat visits

examples.scenario: At 4:40 p.m. Sunday, Luca stands behind the museum membership desk as unused lanyards, visitor stamp pads, and new member cards line the counter. As the visitor-services lead, he has watched the return-offer sign draw polite nods and few second visits. Before Monday reporting, he replaces the launch checklist with an uncertainty checklist about why visitors come back. The second-visit count turns a respected museum launch into a startup-condition test.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the operational checklist, but add an uncertainty checklist for repeat visits. Measure why a stamped visitor returns before expanding the membership campaign.
examples.whyItMatters: The museum's reputation does not answer the new behavior question. Luca defines the experiment by what is unknown, not by the institution's confidence.

questions.prompt: A team inside a century-old bank is building a new tool for first-time borrowers, and nobody knows whether customers will trust automated advice. How should the work be classified?
choices: As startup-condition work because the customer behavior and value are still uncertain.
As routine banking operations because the institution is mature.
As marketing work because trust is mostly a communications problem.
questions.explanation: The bank's age does not settle the customer uncertainty. The work belongs in startup-condition management until trust and value are learned through evidence.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit operations lead is preparing a volunteer scheduling tool for a Saturday food-bank shift. The delivery checklist is clear, but nobody knows whether volunteers will update availability during a busy week. Which first move best applies the definition reset?
choices: Use the same metrics as the existing volunteer program to preserve consistency.
Separate known scheduling logistics from unknown volunteer adoption before choosing metrics.
Brand the tool as innovative so donors understand the ambition.
questions.explanation: The split between known logistics and unknown adoption tells the team what management style to use. Existing metrics and branding can hide the unsettled behavior.

questions.prompt: An agency pilot is judged on whether every milestone lands on the procurement calendar, although resident demand is still unknown. What should the program lead change?
choices: Ask residents to be patient while the procurement process finishes.
Remove timelines entirely because discovery cannot be scheduled.
Add validated-learning evidence to the scorecard so unsettled demand is measured.
questions.explanation: The project still needs dates, but milestones alone grade it like stable work. Validated learning adds evidence about demand without abandoning accountability.

questions.prompt: A museum team assumes a membership experiment should use normal launch standards because the brand is trusted. Which question best tests whether that assumption is wrong?
choices: Will visitors who accept the offer return for a second visit within the test window?
Can the design team produce member cards before opening weekend?
Does the membership desk look consistent with other visitor services?
questions.explanation: Second-visit behavior tests the unsettled value of the membership offer. Cards and desk consistency are execution details inside a more uncertain project.

questions.prompt: A regulated medical device group has clear compliance steps but weak evidence that clinicians want the new workflow. Which plan fits best?
choices: Treat the entire project as compliance execution to reduce risk.
Manage compliance as execution and clinician adoption as uncertainty that needs tested learning.
Delay compliance work until clinicians request the workflow.
questions.explanation: The same project contains known and unknown work. Compliance still needs discipline, while clinician adoption needs a learning metric rather than a finished checklist.

questions.prompt: A manager says, We cannot be doing startup work because we have a legal department and quarterly planning. What is the strongest response?
choices: Startup work requires less planning than large-company work.
Startup work only happens when a team has no stable processes.
Startup work is defined by unsettled facts, not by company size or polish.
questions.explanation: The deciding factor is uncertainty around the new thing being created. Planning and legal structure can coexist with startup work; looseness is not the definition.

questions.prompt: A university service pilot is praised because staff processed every request on time, but no one knows whether students found the service useful enough to return. What went wrong?
choices: The team confused smooth execution with learning in an uncertain service.
The staff should have ignored processing speed until demand was known.
Students should have been required to use the service longer.
questions.explanation: Processing speed may be good execution, but it does not answer the usefulness question. The failure is using a stable-work scorecard for uncertain work.

questions.prompt: A public team argues that calling its project entrepreneurial will make it sound unserious. What deeper issue should the leader address?
choices: Whether the team prefers public-sector language or private-sector language.
Whether the project has unsettled assumptions that require validated learning.
Whether the project can be moved outside government to reduce oversight.
questions.explanation: The label is useful only if it diagnoses uncertainty and changes the scorecard. Language preferences and moving the project do not answer the management-fit question.

questions.prompt: A leadership team must choose between grading a new internal venture by division-level revenue this quarter or by evidence that one customer segment values the offer. Which is the better standard?
choices: Division-level revenue, because internal ventures must prove they can meet mature standards immediately.
A blended score that ignores both revenue and customer evidence until the brand is ready.
Evidence of segment value, because the venture is still discovering whether the offer deserves mature scaling.
questions.explanation: Early uncertain work should be judged by evidence that reduces the main unknown. Mature revenue standards can crush discovery before the team learns what might scale.

reviewCards.front: A project sits inside a large company, but customer demand is unknown. What defines the work?
reviewCards.back: The uncertainty defines it. If the team is creating something new before the key facts are settled, it needs validated learning even when the organization around it is mature.

reviewCards.front: A team treats a new service as routine delivery because the institution is stable. What should you ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask which facts are known and which are still being discovered. Stable context does not make uncertain work stable. The management system has to fit the unknowns.

reviewCards.front: A manager hears “entrepreneur” and thinks hoodie startup. Why does entrepreneurs are everywhere matter for her project?
reviewCards.back: It widens the diagnostic lens. Entrepreneurial work can happen in companies, nonprofits, schools, and government whenever teams create something new under uncertainty.

reviewCards.front: A project contains both compliance tasks and unknown user adoption. How should you manage it?
reviewCards.back: Split the work. Use execution standards for the known compliance tasks and learning standards for the adoption uncertainty. One project can require two scorecards.

reviewCards.front: What is the risk of managing uncertain work with stable-work metrics?
reviewCards.back: The team can look composed while hiding the central unknown. It gets rewarded for predictability before it has learned whether the new thing should exist or how it should work.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to diagnose the condition of the work before choosing the management style. The skill is separating known execution from unsettled discovery so the team is not graded by the wrong scorecard.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a new internal project is being judged by mature-business metrics, then name the unsettled customer facts and propose one validated-learning metric.
If a pilot is treated like routine rollout, then ask which resident or user behavior is still unknown before the launch checklist proceeds.
If donor pressure pushes a fixed plan, then split the wall into known logistics and unknown adoption before committing.
If process discipline is strong but user value is unclear, then manage the regulated tasks normally and create a separate learning test for adoption.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tomorrow, choose one project and draw two columns: known execution and uncertain discovery. Put at least three facts in each, then change one metric to match the discovery column.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review a project that looks settled because of its setting. Ask whether the user, value, channel, or viability facts are actually known. If not, replace one delivery metric with a learning metric.

memorableLines.text: That is startup work when the key facts are still unsettled.
memorableLines.why: The short sentence punctures the assumption that startup work has to look small or informal.

memorableLines.text: The label matters because it changes what good management means.
memorableLines.why: It connects definition to managerial consequences instead of treating the definition as vocabulary.

memorableLines.text: The badge on the door is not the test.
memorableLines.why: It gives the reader a compact way to remember uncertainty over organizational image.

chapters.title: Learn
chapters.hook: Five thank-you emails can feel like proof until the reorder sheet stays blank.
chapters.counterintuition: A smart story feels like learning, but the real test is whether evidence becomes strong enough to alter the next decision.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take one lesson your team claims from recent work and write the evidence beneath it. If the evidence would not change the next decision, rename it a hunch.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Let lessons earn their name: tie every claim to empirical proof and require the next decision to change when the proof changes.

breakdown.fastRead:
Beatrice reads five thank-you emails beside a cooling tray of beans. The roasting team wants to scale the subscription roast next month. The reorder sheet is almost empty.

The room has a pleasant story and a weak lesson.

Validated learning is stricter. It does not ask whether the team can explain a result in a hopeful way. It asks whether evidence proved something true about the customer, product, or business model. A lesson is not validated because the room can explain it well; it is validated when evidence changes what the room does next.
breakdown.deepRead:
Patrick is looking at intake forms marked with skipped fields in blue ink. The front desk says the new mental-health form feels cleaner. Staff frustration is lower. The abandonment tally has barely moved.

That gap matters.

A team can learn language, preferences, and complaints without learning the thing it needs most. Real learning has a job. It reduces uncertainty enough to guide action. If the clinic keeps the new form because staff like it, the decision rests on comfort. If it keeps the form because fewer patients abandon intake, the decision rests on evidence.

Empirical proof does not have to be grand. It can be a cohort, a paid reorder, a completed intake, a second run of a developer tool, or a repair tag that turns into a transaction. The point is that the evidence must answer the claim being made. Praise answers one question. Behavior often answers a harder one.

This is why experimentation matters. It narrows the claim before the result arrives. It says what would count as a lesson and what would merely count as noise. Without that discipline, every launch review becomes a storytelling contest where the most reassuring interpretation wins.

A lesson that changes nothing is still waiting to become evidence.
breakdown.fullRead:
Eva watches a terminal window blink beside a star-count dashboard. The open-source beta has a fresh release tag, a friendly issue thread, and more attention than the maintainers expected. Her hand moves toward the announcement draft. Then she opens the usage logs and checks how many starred users returned to run the tool twice.

The number is smaller than the applause.

Validated learning has an uncomfortable center: the claim must be tied to the behavior it pretends to describe. If the team claims developers find the tool useful, then stars and kind issues may be clues, but repeated use is closer to proof. If the team claims a bakery buyer wants weekly ordering, then one cheerful email is not the same as a weekly order form filled out again. If the team claims riders value repair, then conversations at a tent are not the same as paid tuneups on the payment reader.

What would you stop doing if the evidence failed?

That question protects learning from becoming theater. A claim deserves more trust when the team can name the action that will change if the claim is wrong. Otherwise the result can be admired, discussed, and filed away while the next decision stays exactly as planned.

David faces that moment in a bakery packing room. A flour-dusted invoice sits on the table, and the buyer email is warm enough to make the whole team smile. The delivery route note has space for a weekly account. David separates the pleasant message from validated demand. Before the next batch schedule is approved, he needs the buyer to complete the weekly order form, not merely praise the first delivery.

The same discipline applies when the problem is failure rather than demand. Lars sees three red conflicts on the lab booking calendar. The team has solved each late-return fight as a separate incident. Then he runs the Five Whys and keeps going past the obvious explanation. When the same fault keeps returning, the fifth why often points away from the bug and toward the system that keeps making it. In this case, the equipment cabinet key changes hands without an owner, and the handoff note is optional. The recurring conflict was not a student attitude problem. It was a system with a missing joint.

Root-cause thinking belongs with validated learning because both refuse easy interpretation. They push past the first satisfying answer. They ask what evidence would prove the claim and what cause would keep the failure from returning.

There is a limit. Teams should not demand laboratory certainty before making every move. That would turn learning into delay. The standard is practical: evidence strong enough for the decision at hand. A low-risk copy change may need a small signal. A business model change needs more. The proof should match the cost of being wrong.

Learning is not the warm feeling after a useful conversation. It is the moment evidence earns the authority to steer.

examples.title: Beatrice Checks the Reorder Sheet

planSpec.stakes: friendly comments could be mistaken for proof of repeat demand
planSpec.requiredBeat: Beatrice compares compliments with reorder behavior before approving a bigger roast

examples.scenario: At 6:35 a.m. Friday, Beatrice stands beside a cooling tray of beans and five thank-you emails taped near the roast calendar. The team wants to approve a bigger subscription roast before lunch. The sample bags drew praise, but the reorder sheet has only two names. Beatrice must choose between scaling the roast and treating the compliments as clues until repeat demand appears. The reorder sheet has to decide the roast schedule before praise turns into extra inventory.
examples.whatToDo: Compare the praise with reorder behavior before approving more beans. Make the next roast size depend on actual repeat orders, not on how good the first reactions felt.
examples.whyItMatters: Friendly comments can lift morale without proving demand. The reorder sheet connects the claimed lesson to customer behavior that can change the roasting decision.

examples.title: Patrick Challenges the Cleaner Form

planSpec.stakes: lower staff frustration may not prove patient completion improved
planSpec.requiredBeat: Patrick asks whether the changed form reduced abandoned intakes or merely felt cleaner

examples.scenario: "Did fewer patients finish, or did we just feel better?" Patrick asks at the front desk, holding a clipboard with skipped fields in blue ink. The intake forms look cleaner, and the front-desk notes are calmer. The abandonment tally is still open on the screen. Before the clinic keeps the redesign, Patrick must decide whether to accept staff comfort as learning or require evidence that more patients complete intake. The skipped-field tally gives Patrick a patient behavior signal that staff comfort cannot replace.
examples.whatToDo: Put the abandonment tally beside the staff notes. Keep the form only if patient completion improved, or run a sharper test on the fields patients still skip.
examples.whyItMatters: Staff relief is real, but it proves a different claim. The clinic needs evidence that the redesign changed patient behavior, not only the staff's experience.

examples.title: Eva Opens the Usage Logs

planSpec.stakes: GitHub stars may flatter the team without proving usage
planSpec.requiredBeat: Eva checks whether starred users returned to run the tool twice

examples.scenario: The terminal window glows beside a star-count dashboard while Eva scrolls past a warm issue thread and the latest release tag. The maintainer group is ready to call the beta validated. Her cursor pauses over the usage logs. She has a decision to make: celebrate the stars or check whether starred users came back to run the tool twice. The usage logs decide whether the release tag created actual repeat use or only public attention.
examples.whatToDo: Open the usage logs before writing the success note. Treat stars and comments as attention, then test usefulness by repeat runs from the same developers.
examples.whyItMatters: Stars can flatter a maintainer group while leaving value unproved. Repeat use is closer to the claim that developers found the tool worth adopting.

examples.title: David Separates Email From Weekly Demand

planSpec.stakes: one successful order may become a story the team wants too much
planSpec.requiredBeat: David separates a pleasant buyer email from validated demand for weekly ordering

examples.scenario: You are at the packing table with David, where a flour-dusted invoice sits under a warm buyer email. The weekly order form is still blank, and the delivery route note has room for a standing account. Before the oven schedule is expanded, David needs to decide whether one pleasant order proves demand or whether weekly ordering has to earn that claim. The weekly order form is the behavior that earns a bigger oven schedule.
examples.whatToDo: Ask for the weekly order form before changing the batch schedule. Keep the buyer email as encouragement, but do not let it stand in for validated demand.
examples.whyItMatters: A successful first order can become a story the team wants to believe. Weekly commitment is the evidence that can safely change production.

examples.title: Manon Counts Paid Tuneups After the Rain

planSpec.stakes: busy foot traffic might hide whether riders value paid repair
planSpec.requiredBeat: Manon counts actual paid tuneups instead of conversations at the tent

examples.scenario: At 5:15 p.m. Saturday, Manon folds the rain tarp behind the city-bike pop-up on Queen Street. Repair tags flutter from the curbside rack, and dozens of riders have chatted about safer cycling. As the program coordinator, she checks the payment reader before the debrief and counts nine paid tuneups instead of treating all those conversations as proof of demand. The payment reader keeps Manon focused on repair demand instead of awareness.
examples.whatToDo: Use the payment reader as the proof for paid repair demand. Record conversations as leads, but base the next pop-up on actual tuneups purchased.
examples.whyItMatters: Foot traffic can make a nonprofit feel useful while the business question stays open. Paid tuneups show whether riders value the service enough to act.

examples.title: Lars Runs Five Whys on the Booking Calendar

planSpec.stakes: solving a visible booking conflict may miss the repeated root cause
planSpec.requiredBeat: Lars runs Five Whys until the team sees the ownership gap behind late returns

examples.scenario: At 7:50 a.m. Wednesday, Lars stands in the university lab office with three red microscope-booking conflicts on the calendar and the equipment cabinet key missing again. As lab manager, he has already sent two reminder emails. Before sending a third, he runs Five Whys with the administrators and finds that nobody owns the key handoff between evening users and morning staff. The missing handoff owner gives Lars a system cause to change before another reminder email goes out.
examples.whatToDo: Keep asking why until the repeated conflict points to a system cause. Change the key handoff owner instead of sending another reminder about late returns.
examples.whyItMatters: Fixing the visible conflict can feel like learning while the cause keeps producing the same failure. Five Whys turns the postmortem into correction.

questions.prompt: A team says it learned customers love a new service because several pilot users sent kind notes, but none used it again. What is missing?
choices: Evidence tied to the claim, such as repeat use or another behavior that would change the next decision.
A larger pile of encouraging comments from the same kind of users.
A longer meeting where the team can discuss what the comments mean.
questions.explanation: The claim is about customer value, so behavior must support it. More comments and longer interpretation can still leave the decision resting on hope.

questions.prompt: A clinic redesign lowers staff complaints, but patient intake abandonment barely changes. Which next move best fits validated learning?
choices: Keep the redesign because staff experience is part of patient care.
Run a focused test on the fields patients still skip and measure completion.
Add more explanatory text to every section of the form.
questions.explanation: The decision should follow evidence about patient completion, the claim being tested. Staff relief matters, but it proves a different outcome.

questions.prompt: An open-source team receives a surge of stars after launch. Which measurement would best test whether the tool is actually useful?
choices: How quickly the star count rose during the launch day.
How many maintainers felt encouraged by the issue thread.
How many starred users return and run the tool again within the next week.
questions.explanation: Repeat use is evidence for usefulness. Star velocity and team morale may be encouraging, but neither proves developers adopted the tool.

questions.prompt: A bakery owner has one warm wholesale email on the packing table and a blank recurring-order form beside the flour scale. The team wants to expand next week's production schedule before the buyer commits again. What should happen first?
choices: Ask the buyer to complete a weekly order form or place another recurring order.
Publish the buyer email on the bakery's website.
Increase production slightly because enthusiasm is time-sensitive.
questions.explanation: Recurring ordering tests the demand claim that would justify production changes. Publicity and small expansion still lean on a single pleasant story.

questions.prompt: A city-bike nonprofit reports hundreds of friendly tent conversations after a rainy Saturday pop-up, but the payment reader shows only a few tuneups. The board wants to call the event validated. Which lesson is safest?
choices: Cyclists dislike the mission because paid demand was low.
Conversation volume showed awareness, while paid tuneups are the better test of repair demand.
The pop-up should be repeated unchanged because foot traffic was high.
questions.explanation: Conversation and payment answer different questions. The safe lesson separates awareness from willingness to pay instead of overclaiming either signal.

questions.prompt: A lab keeps sending reminder emails after late equipment returns, but conflicts keep appearing on the booking calendar. What does Five Whys add?
choices: It creates a neutral way to blame the student who used the equipment last.
It delays correction until the team has complete certainty about every incident.
It helps the team find the recurring system cause instead of treating each late return as a separate mistake.
questions.explanation: Five Whys pushes beyond the visible incident toward the system producing repeats. It is not a blame ritual or an excuse to postpone action.

questions.prompt: A product group keeps every planned feature after a launch review, even though the evidence contradicted the team's demand story. What does that reveal?
choices: The team may be discussing results without letting learning change decisions.
The evidence was not useful unless the team had a perfect experiment.
The planned features must have strategic value outside customer demand.
questions.explanation: Validated learning should affect the next move. If the plan stays intact after contradictory evidence, the review may be interpretation theater.

questions.prompt: A team has interview quotes, a small usage bump, and one paid order. They want to claim the business model works. What is the best analysis?
choices: Any paid order validates the full business model because money changed hands.
The signals may be useful, but the claim is too broad unless evidence proves the specific business model assumption.
Interview quotes are more reliable than behavior because customers explain intent.
questions.explanation: Evidence has to match the claim. One paid order may prove willingness in a narrow case, but it does not automatically validate the whole model.

questions.prompt: A team must choose between declaring victory from positive demo reactions or running a narrower test that could disprove its favorite assumption. Which is stronger?
choices: Declare victory because confidence helps the team keep momentum.
Avoid both options until market conditions are easier to interpret.
Run the narrower test because learning counts when evidence can challenge and redirect the plan.
questions.explanation: The narrower test gives reality a chance to change the decision. Demo reactions may help morale, but they are weak if they cannot redirect the plan.

reviewCards.front: A team says it learned something after launch. What must you check before trusting the claim?
reviewCards.back: Check whether evidence supports the specific claim and whether the next decision changes because of it. If nothing changes, the team may have a story rather than validated learning.

reviewCards.front: Why are compliments weak proof for customer value?
reviewCards.back: Compliments show reaction, not necessarily behavior. Customer value usually needs evidence closer to use, return, payment, completion, or another action tied to the claim.

reviewCards.front: A repeated failure keeps getting patched. What question should pull the team deeper?
reviewCards.back: Ask why the failure keeps returning until the cause points to a system, habit, or handoff the team can change. The goal is correction, not a better incident story.

reviewCards.front: What makes a launch review become theater instead of learning?
reviewCards.back: It becomes theater when people interpret results in a comforting way while preserving the same plan. Learning needs evidence with authority over the next decision.

reviewCards.front: How much proof does a team need before acting?
reviewCards.back: Enough proof for the cost of the decision. Small changes can use smaller signals. Expensive or business-model decisions need stronger evidence because being wrong costs more.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to make claimed lessons answerable. The skill is matching each claim to evidence, then requiring the next decision to respond when the evidence is weak, strong, or surprising.

ifThenPlans.plan: If someone says we learned that customers want it, then ask which behavior proved that exact claim and what decision will change because of it.
If interviews sound encouraging, then separate what people said from what they did before changing the roadmap.
If the same issue returns for the third time, then run Five Whys until the cause points to a system change, not another reminder.
If a positive signal arrives after a hard week, then enjoy it briefly and still ask whether it proves the claim the team wants to make.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tomorrow, pick one claimed lesson from recent work. Under it, write the exact evidence, the decision it affects, and what you would do differently if the evidence were false.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of each week, choose one result and classify it as encouragement, clue, or validated learning. Promote it only if the evidence is strong enough to steer a real decision.

memorableLines.text: The room has a pleasant story and a weak lesson.
memorableLines.why: It separates morale from evidence in a concrete way.

memorableLines.text: A lesson that changes nothing is still waiting to become evidence.
memorableLines.why: It captures the chapter's demand that learning alter decisions.

memorableLines.text: The number is smaller than the applause.
memorableLines.why: It makes the difference between attention and validated behavior instantly visible.

chapters.title: Experiment
chapters.hook: A survey can praise the idea while a pickup table quietly refuses it.
chapters.counterintuition: Research is not learning, but a way to shape the live test. The stronger move is to ask for behavior the team cannot politely explain away.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one belief as a testable sentence: We believe users will do X when offered Y. Then choose the smallest live behavior that can prove or weaken it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Turn hopeful beliefs into experiments where real behavior tests value or growth before opinions harden into plans.

breakdown.fastRead:
Grace has a survey printout full of praise for the farm-share pickup redesign. Members like the idea of faster pickup. They like the chalkboard menu. They like the sample cooler near the crates.

Friday is where the claim must go.

A value test asks whether people do the thing that proves the offer matters, not whether they compliment the idea. Grace turns the preference survey into a pickup-token test. If members change how they collect food when the new setup is real, the team learns something. If they only praised it on paper, the plan has been spared a larger mistake.
breakdown.deepRead:
"Would you invite a friend to unlock the next lesson?" Nicolas asks while the phone shows an unsent invite. The mobile team has heard users say they like the language app. That answer is not enough for a Growth hypothesis. A growth story stays fiction until an experiment shows how one user reliably leads to another.

The test is narrow: send one real invite to unlock one lesson.

Experiments do not have to be elaborate. They have to be honest about the claim. If the claim is value, the test should ask for behavior that shows the offer matters. If the claim is growth, the test should ask whether use creates more use, referral, retention, or paid acquisition. Market research can help shape the test, but it cannot replace the moment when a person has to act.

This is why a live test often beats another round of opinions. Opinions carry politeness, imagination, and the desire to be helpful. Behavior carries friction. A user either sends the invite, reserves the material, books the appointment, buys the bundle, or uploads the photo.

Actionable feedback comes from the friction.

Nicolas writes the referral claim on a sticky note before anyone opens the research deck. The claim is not that learners enjoy the app. The claim is that one learner will spend social trust to bring in another. That makes the test sharper: one invite, one unlock, one tally the team cannot soften with encouraging comments.
breakdown.fullRead:
Rachel looks at a stack of vaccination postcards beside the reception phone. Pet owners told the clinic that reminders would help. The booking log says many still schedule late. She can keep asking whether people like reminders, or she can send one SMS script to a small group and watch whether appointments move sooner.

That choice turns research into experiment.

The distinction matters because teams often confuse better language about the customer with better evidence from the customer. Interviews can reveal worries, vocabulary, and context. Surveys can show preference. Neither is useless. The problem begins when the team treats stated preference as if it were tested behavior. Under uncertainty, the important question is not whether the idea sounds attractive. It is whether people act when the offer enters their real day.

What behavior would make the claim harder to dodge?

Marco has to answer that at a circular-economy salvage table. Builders admire the reclaimed brass handle and ask for more material photos. Admiration is cheap compared with reserving inventory. So he asks for a small hold deposit before the reservation deadline, not another interview about reuse. The deposit form is uncomfortable because it turns approval into commitment. That is exactly why it teaches.

There are two core questions running through this kind of work. The Value hypothesis asks whether people care enough to use, pay, return, reserve, or otherwise behave as if the offer matters. The Growth hypothesis asks whether that use can create more use through retention, referral, acquisition, or another mechanism. Each hypothesis needs a test that can produce a visible result.

Astrid learns this in the theatre box office. Audience members say a two-show bundle sounds charming. The weekend window tells the truth more clearly. She puts color-coded tickets in the drawer, offers the bundle for two nights, and checks the sales sheet. If people still buy single nights, the bundle praise was only a clue. If they buy pairs, the theatre has evidence to build on.

The counterweight is important: do not worship experiments as if every decision needs a perfect trial. Some choices are too small to overtest. Some early tests will be rough. The standard is not scientific theater. The standard is whether the test puts the key belief into contact with reality soon enough to affect the next move.

Connor sees the same rule in a diabetes meal-planning service. Clinicians approve the handout, but patients may still ignore it after the consult. The team watches one upload metric: does the patient send a real dinner photo when prompted that night? A handout can earn professional approval and still fail in a kitchen. The photo prompt makes value visible where the behavior actually happens.

An experiment is a question with consequences. If the answer cannot change the plan, the team has not tested the belief. It has only decorated it.

examples.title: Grace Moves the Survey to Friday Pickup

planSpec.stakes: survey praise may not prove members will change pickup behavior
planSpec.requiredBeat: Grace turns a preference survey into a Friday pickup behavior test

examples.scenario: At 4:05 p.m. Friday, Grace sets a chalkboard menu against produce crates and clips the survey printout beside a bowl of pickup tokens. Members praised the redesign, but the sample cooler will show whether they actually choose the faster route. Before the line forms, Grace must choose between trusting stated preference and running the pickup behavior test. The pickup tokens make the test visible because each member chooses a real route under Friday pressure.
examples.whatToDo: Run the Friday pickup test with tokens and the sample cooler. Use actual route choices to decide whether the redesign matters beyond survey praise.
examples.whyItMatters: The survey shows what members liked imagining. Pickup behavior shows whether the redesign changes a real handoff when people are tired and carrying groceries.

examples.title: Nicolas Locks One Lesson Behind a Real Invite

planSpec.stakes: users may like the concept but never invite a friend
planSpec.requiredBeat: Nicolas sets a test where learners must send one real invite to unlock a lesson

examples.scenario: "Do they say they would invite someone, or do they send the invite?" Nicolas asks at 2:20 p.m. in the language-app team room, holding a phone screen with an unsent invite and an invite code. The lesson lock is ready for a small user group, and the referral tally is blank. Before the sprint starts, the team has to choose between more concept feedback and a test where one real invite unlocks one lesson. The invite code must turn praise into a measurable act before the team calls the growth claim real.
examples.whatToDo: Put the lesson lock in front of a small user group and require a real invite. Judge the growth idea by the referral tally, not by verbal approval.
examples.whyItMatters: A growth hypothesis needs behavior that creates another user. Liking the concept does not show whether learners will spend social capital on an invite.

examples.title: Rachel Sends One Reminder Script

planSpec.stakes: pet owners may say reminders help without booking sooner
planSpec.requiredBeat: Rachel tests one reminder script against actual appointment bookings

examples.scenario: The vaccination postcards sit in a rubber-banded stack by the reception phone while Rachel studies the booking log. Pet owners said reminders would help, and the SMS script sounds friendly. Her thumb hovers over the send button. She needs to decide whether to keep asking for opinions or test whether one script moves actual appointments sooner. The booking log gives Rachel a before-and-after signal tied to appointment dates, not reminder opinions.
examples.whatToDo: Send the SMS script to a small group and compare booking dates with the usual postcard group. Let appointment movement judge the reminder service.
examples.whyItMatters: Pet owners can endorse reminders without changing behavior. The booking log shows whether the reminder creates action while the vaccine date still matters.

examples.title: Marco Asks for a Hold Deposit

planSpec.stakes: builders may admire reuse but not reserve materials
planSpec.requiredBeat: Marco asks for a hold deposit instead of another interview

examples.scenario: You are beside Marco at a salvage-market sample table in Rotterdam, where a reclaimed brass handle rests next to material photos and a deposit form. Builders keep praising reuse, but the reservation deadline is tomorrow. Before packing the samples, Marco must decide whether to book another interview or ask for a small hold deposit that proves someone will reserve the materials. The deposit form makes commitment visible before the scarce material is promised to anyone else.
examples.whatToDo: Ask for the hold deposit before scheduling more interviews. Use reservations, not admiration, to test whether the marketplace has value to builders.
examples.whyItMatters: Admiration costs builders nothing. A deposit exposes whether reuse matters enough to claim scarce materials before the deadline passes.

examples.title: Astrid Tests the Two-Show Bundle

planSpec.stakes: audiences may like bundles but still buy single nights
planSpec.requiredBeat: Astrid runs a two-show bundle at the box office for one weekend

examples.scenario: It took Astrid one weekend window to separate charm from buying. The box-office drawer held color-coded tickets, and the sales sheet tracked singles beside the new ticket bundle. Patrons smiled at the ticket-window offer on Friday. By Sunday, the sheet showed whether they actually bought two-show plans or returned to single nights. The sales sheet forces the theatre to separate friendly box-office talk from paired-ticket purchases.
examples.whatToDo: Run the bundle for one weekend and read the sales sheet before expanding it. Treat smiles as interest and paired purchases as the behavior that matters.
examples.whyItMatters: Audience approval can be polite and cheap. The box office shows whether the bundle changes a purchase when real money and calendar time are involved.

examples.title: Connor Watches for One Dinner Photo

planSpec.stakes: clinicians may approve the plan while patients ignore it
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sam watches whether patients upload one real dinner photo after the consult

examples.scenario: The phone gallery is open to a dinner plate beside the clinician handout. Before, Connor's team treated clinical approval as proof the meal plan was strong. After adding a photo prompt after each consult, the upload metric tells a sharper story: patients either send one real dinner photo that night or the service has not entered their routine. The dinner photo is the first behavior that shows whether the plan survives outside the clinic.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the clinician handout, but test the patient behavior with a dinner photo prompt. Use uploads after the consult as the first value signal.
examples.whyItMatters: Professional approval does not prove patient use. A real dinner photo shows whether the plan survives the evening when choices are made.

questions.prompt: A team has survey data showing users like a feature concept, but no one has tried it in a real workflow. What is the missing step?
choices: A live experiment where user behavior can answer the value claim.
A larger survey with more demographic detail.
A stronger presentation of the survey findings.
questions.explanation: The value claim needs behavior, not only stated preference. More survey detail may shape the test, but it cannot replace a live result.

questions.prompt: A language app team believes referrals will drive growth because learners say they would invite friends, but nobody has sent an invite from inside the product. Which experiment tests that belief most directly?
choices: Ask learners in interviews whether they would recommend the app.
Require a small group to send one real invite to unlock a lesson and track completed invites.
Rewrite the referral copy until the team agrees it sounds natural.
questions.explanation: The real invite tests whether one user can lead to another. Interviews and copy reviews may help, but they do not show referral behavior.

questions.prompt: A clinic owner wants to know whether pet owners will book vaccinations sooner after reminders. Which measure belongs in the experiment?
choices: How many owners say reminders sound useful.
How attractive the reminder postcard looks at reception.
Whether owners who receive the script book earlier than the comparison group.
questions.explanation: Earlier booking is the behavior tied to the claim. Usefulness ratings and design quality can inform the message, but the booking log carries the test.

questions.prompt: A salvage marketplace hears builders praise reclaimed materials, but reservations stay vague. What should the team test next?
choices: Ask for a small hold deposit before the reservation deadline.
Interview more builders about why reuse matters.
Add more photos to the material gallery.
questions.explanation: The deposit turns admiration into commitment. Interviews and photos may increase interest, but the value hypothesis needs a reservation behavior.

questions.prompt: A health startup's meal plan is approved by clinicians, but patients rarely use it after leaving the consult. Which test best targets value?
choices: Ask clinicians to rate the handout again after revisions.
Add a prompt asking patients to upload one dinner photo that evening.
Make the handout more visually polished.
questions.explanation: A dinner upload tests patient use in the setting that matters. Clinician ratings and polish do not prove the plan enters the patient's routine.

questions.prompt: A theatre audience says a ticket bundle sounds appealing, but the arts manager is unsure. Why is a one-weekend box-office test stronger than another survey?
choices: It creates urgency that makes any offer look more successful.
It removes the need to understand why patrons choose single nights.
It tests actual purchase behavior under the same constraints as the real offer.
questions.explanation: The weekend test asks patrons to spend money and calendar time, which matches the claim. Urgency and ignorance of motives are not the mechanism.

questions.prompt: A product team says its market research proves customers want the service. The research is all interviews and preference rankings. What should you question?
choices: Whether the team has turned the belief into a behavior test that can produce actionable feedback.
Whether interviews should ever be used in uncertain product work.
Whether customers are qualified to describe their own preferences.
questions.explanation: Research can help frame the hypothesis, but a behavior test is needed for actionable feedback. The issue is not banning interviews or dismissing customers.

questions.prompt: A team tests three changes at once: price, referral reward, and onboarding flow. The conversion rate rises slightly. What makes the result hard to use?
choices: The result is invalid because only large experiments produce learning.
The team cannot tell which hypothesis the behavior answered.
The team should have used opinions instead of behavior.
questions.explanation: The mixed test blurs the link between behavior and hypothesis. Small experiments can teach, and behavior is still stronger than opinion when designed cleanly.

questions.prompt: A founder can either run another round of concept interviews or ask ten interested users to make a small paid reservation this week. Which better tests value?
choices: The interviews, because they provide richer language about the idea.
Neither, because value cannot be tested before a finished product exists.
The paid reservation, because it turns interest into behavior with a consequence.
questions.explanation: The reservation better tests whether the offer matters enough to act. Interviews may be rich, but they do not carry the same consequence.

reviewCards.front: A survey says people like an idea. What makes it an experiment?
reviewCards.back: A real behavior has to answer the claim. Turn the idea into a test where people use, pay, reserve, invite, return, or otherwise act under real constraints.

reviewCards.front: How do you distinguish a value hypothesis from a growth hypothesis?
reviewCards.back: A value hypothesis asks whether people care enough to use or pay. A growth hypothesis asks whether use can create more use through retention, referral, acquisition, or another mechanism.

reviewCards.front: A team wants more interviews before testing. What should you ask?
