reviewCards.back: Ask what behavior the interviews are meant to prepare. Research is useful when it sharpens the experiment, not when it postpones contact with reality.

reviewCards.front: Why should an experiment be narrow?
reviewCards.back: A narrow experiment keeps the link between hypothesis and result clear. If too many things change at once, behavior may move without teaching the team which belief was right or wrong.

reviewCards.front: What makes feedback actionable?
reviewCards.back: It is actionable when the result can change the next decision. Praise, opinions, and traffic can be useful clues, but an experiment needs a result with consequences.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to convert beliefs into tests. The skill is naming whether you are testing value or growth, then choosing a live behavior that can answer before the team commits more work.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a survey result sounds encouraging, then write the behavior that would prove it in the real world before changing the plan.
If someone predicts referrals, then run a small invite test with a real referral tally instead of debating the concept.
If users say a new process is better, then test whether they use it when the old process is still available.
If people praise the offer, then ask for a small commitment, reservation, purchase, or return visit that matches the claim.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tomorrow, pick one hopeful belief and rewrite it as either a value hypothesis or growth hypothesis. Choose one live behavior that could answer it this week.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review one piece of research and ask what experiment it should create. Do not let interviews, surveys, or opinions count as proof until behavior tests the claim.

memorableLines.why: It moves the reader from opinion to live behavior in one concrete phrase.

memorableLines.text: Actionable feedback comes from the friction.
memorableLines.why: It explains why behavior teaches more than polite answers.

memorableLines.text: An experiment is a question with consequences.
memorableLines.why: It gives the chapter's method a memorable test for seriousness.

chapters.title: Leap
chapters.hook: The prettiest boot rack in the hotel lobby still rests on one unproved bet.
chapters.counterintuition: Listing assumptions looks responsible; the hidden cost is letting the dangerous one stay protected unless the first test targets the belief that could break the plan.
chapters.tryThisNow: Choose one project and write the assumption that could break it. Put a star beside that line and design the next test around only that risk.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Name the leap your plan depends on, rank it by damage if false, and test the business-breaking assumption first.

breakdown.fastRead:
Laura's boot rack looks perfect beside the ski-town hotel door. The rental tags are crisp. The hotel desk card is clear. The deposit amount has been debated for an hour.

One belief carries the whole plan: tourists will rent winter boots instead of buying them.

The leap is the belief holding the plan up before proof has arrived. Smaller questions can wait. If tourists will not rent, better signage and cleaner tags do not save the model. The riskiest assumption deserves the first test because it decides whether the rest of the work matters.
breakdown.deepRead:
"Trust goes in the top slot," Etienne says while a calendar alert hovers over a tax folder. The fintech team wants to build bank-link integrations for freelancer tax reminders. The bank-link mockup looks impressive. The manual reminder can test the risk sooner: will freelancers trust an automated nudge about taxes before connecting an account?

Leap-of-faith assumptions are the load-bearing beliefs the plan quietly stands on while the team still lacks proof.

Every uncertain project has many assumptions. Some are annoying if false. Some are fatal. The work begins when the team ranks the difference. Menu preferences matter for a meal service, but payer commitment may matter more. Training videos matter for safety education, but supervisor release may matter first. Clause automation matters for legal tools, but client willingness to pay for human review may determine whether automation is valuable at all.

The value hypothesis and growth hypothesis often contain the biggest leaps. Do people care enough to use or pay? Can the business find more of them in a repeatable way? Those questions steer because they sit under everything else.

Polish should not arrive before the floor is tested.
breakdown.fullRead:
Emily clips a sample menu to a fridge magnet and studies the payer call list. The meals have been tested for nutrition, the packaging looks gentle, and families say variety matters. The monthly price is the heavier question. If adult children will not pay every month, the menu debate is decoration.

She calls five payers before approving another recipe cycle.

Riskiest assumption first is the rule: the first test belongs to the assumption that would make every polished detail irrelevant if it failed. That sounds obvious until a team is close to the work. People naturally drift toward assumptions they know how to improve: copy, features, colors, schedules, menu choices, video quality. The lethal assumption often feels rude to test because it threatens the whole project.

What is the belief you keep improving around?

Pavel sees the same pattern at a manufacturing plant. The HR team wants to film safety micro-training modules, but the punch clock and shift roster point to a deeper risk. Supervisors may not release workers for five minutes. The training tablet can be perfect and still sit unused. Pavel tests the release slip before filming, because access to five minutes is the business-breaking assumption for that version of the program.

Assumption ranking is not pessimism. It is steering. A team cannot steer with twenty equal worries. It needs to know which belief gets tested first, which can wait, and which is already known well enough for now. The danger is turning the assumption list into paperwork: a table filled out once, admired for its completeness, and ignored while the team builds around the scariest line.

Maja learns this with a childcare swap. The matching features are easy to imagine. The harder leap is trust. At her kitchen table, printed emergency contacts and a two-family cap sit beside a trial evening form. In the postmortem, she names reciprocal care as the real leap and asks two families to try one evening before building a matching system. The small test may feel humble, but it touches the load-bearing belief.

There is a limit to fear-based ranking. If every assumption is called fatal, the team freezes. The ranking has to be practical: which false belief would make the current plan collapse or change shape dramatically? Test that one. If it survives, move to the next. If it fails, be grateful that it failed while the cost was still small.

Jack faces the question with a legal-document automation tool. A marked-up contract sits beside a payment link and a review option. Clients may like automation but still demand a lawyer's eyes before signing. He tests paid review preference before automating every clause. If human review is the value, automation has to serve that reality rather than replace it in a fantasy.

A leap is not a flaw in the plan. It is the honest place where the plan admits it does not know enough yet. Put the weight there first.

examples.title: Laura Marks the Boot Rental Leap

planSpec.stakes: inventory plans collapse if tourists will not rent instead of buy
planSpec.requiredBeat: Laura marks rental willingness as the business-breaking assumption and tests it first

The hotel desk card explains the offer, and the deposit amount is still circled on her clipboard. Before ordering more sizes, she must choose whether to test rental willingness first or keep polishing the kiosk setup. The first rental request is the only signal that can justify polishing the tags.
examples.whatToDo: Make rental willingness the first test. Put a small set of boots at the desk, use the deposit amount, and measure whether tourists rent before buying inventory.
examples.whyItMatters: If tourists will not rent boots, the rest of the kiosk plan collapses. Testing that leap first protects the team from perfecting a display for a false belief.

examples.title: Etienne Puts Trust Above Integrations

planSpec.stakes: the model fails if users will not trust automated tax nudges
planSpec.requiredBeat: Etienne puts trust in the riskiest-assumption slot before building integrations

examples.scenario: "The bank link can wait," Etienne says as a calendar alert hovers over a tax folder on the laptop. The trust survey is thin, the manual reminder is ready, and the bank-link mockup is getting all the attention. Before the sprint locks, he has to choose between building integrations and testing whether freelancers trust automated tax nudges at all. The manual reminder lets Etienne test trust before the bank-link build becomes the center of the plan.
examples.whatToDo: Run the manual reminder test before the bank-link build. Measure trust through responses and opt-ins, then decide whether integrations deserve engineering time.
examples.whyItMatters: The model fails if freelancers distrust the nudge. Integration polish cannot rescue a service whose riskiest assumption is that users will accept the advice.

examples.title: Emily Calls the Monthly Payers First

planSpec.requiredBeat: Emily tests payer commitment before menu variety

The monthly price is printed in bold, and every recipe conversation feels easier than asking adult children to commit. As program lead, she has to choose whether to approve another recipe cycle or call five payers about monthly payment first. The payer call list makes monthly commitment visible before another menu cycle absorbs the week.
examples.whatToDo: Call the payers before changing the menu. Ask for monthly commitment at the real price, then use the answer to decide whether recipe work is worth expanding.
examples.whyItMatters: Nutrition preferences matter only after the payer leap survives. If adult children will not pay monthly, menu variety is a secondary problem.

examples.title: Pavel Tests the Five-Minute Release

planSpec.stakes: course polish is wasted if supervisors will not release workers for five minutes
planSpec.requiredBeat: Pavel tests supervisor release before filming modules

examples.scenario: You are with Pavel beside the punch clock, where a training tablet sits under the shift roster and a release slip waits for supervisor initials. The HR team wants to film the first safety module this week. Before the camera is booked, Pavel has to decide whether to test supervisor release for five minutes or polish the course script. The release slip is the real gate because training cannot work without five supervisor-approved minutes.
examples.whatToDo: Ask supervisors to release workers for one five-minute test before filming. Treat signed release slips as the first proof the micro-training can reach the floor.
examples.whyItMatters: Course quality is wasted if workers never get access. The release slip tests the assumption that controls whether the rest of the training can matter.

examples.title: Maja Names Trust as the Childcare Leap

planSpec.stakes: matching features fail if parents do not trust reciprocal care
planSpec.requiredBeat: Maja names trust as the leap and asks families for one trial evening

examples.scenario: It took Maja one kitchen-table postmortem to admit the matching features were not the hard part. Printed emergency contacts, a contact sheet, and a two-family cap sat beside the trial evening form. The first parents liked the idea, but trust would decide everything. Maja names trust as the leap and asks two families to try one evening. The trial evening tests trust directly while the matching software remains only a later option.
examples.whatToDo: Test reciprocal trust with one capped trial evening before building matching features. Use emergency contacts and a clear form to make the trust question visible.
examples.whyItMatters: Matching software cannot create trust after the fact. If parents will not try one evening, feature work only decorates a broken assumption.

examples.title: Jack Tests Paid Review Before Clause Automation

planSpec.stakes: automation value fails if clients still demand human review
planSpec.requiredBeat: Jack tests paid review preference before automating every clause

examples.scenario: A marked-up contract lies beside a payment link and a review option on Jack's desk. Before, he planned to automate every clause because clients wanted speed. After three prospects ask who checks the draft, he tests paid review preference first. The next build depends on whether clients choose automation alone or pay for a lawyer's eyes. The payment link tells Jack whether human review is the load-bearing value before clause automation expands.
examples.whatToDo: Offer the review option before automating more clauses. Measure whether clients pay for human review, then shape the tool around the value they choose.
examples.whyItMatters: If clients still demand human review, automation must support that trust need. Testing the preference first prevents Jack from building around the wrong value.

questions.prompt: A team has ten assumptions on a planning sheet before a Monday build review: button color, email tone, onboarding copy, payment trust, and several feature details. Which one should get the first test?
choices: The assumption whose failure would make the current plan collapse.
The easiest assumption to test quickly.
The assumption that produces the most interesting discussion.
questions.explanation: The first test belongs to the assumption with the highest damage if false. Ease and discussion value can distract from the load-bearing risk.

questions.prompt: A boot-rental team is debating tag design and deposit wording at a ski-town hotel before knowing whether tourists will rent boots instead of buying them. What should they do next?
choices: Finalize the tag design so the offer feels professional.
Run a small rental test at the hotel desk with a real deposit.
Order more sizes to make the test look complete.
questions.explanation: Rental willingness is the leap that can break the kiosk. Tag design and inventory matter later if tourists actually rent.

questions.prompt: A fintech team wants to build bank integrations for freelancer tax reminders, but the riskiest belief is whether users will trust an automated nudge before linking an account. Which test should come first?
choices: Build the integrations because trust grows when the product is complete.
Ask the design team to make the reminder screen friendlier.
Send manual reminders to a small group and measure trust, replies, and opt-ins.
questions.explanation: Manual reminders test the risky trust assumption before engineering spend. Completion and friendliness cannot fix a service users will not trust.

questions.prompt: A meal-delivery founder keeps improving menus, but the business depends on adult children paying monthly. Which move handles the riskiest assumption?
choices: Test payer commitment at the monthly price before expanding menu variety.
Survey seniors about their favorite meals before calling payers.
Add more meal photos so the offer feels easier to understand.
questions.explanation: Payer commitment is the dangerous leap for the model. Preferences and photos are useful only after the payment assumption has evidence.

questions.prompt: A manufacturing HR team wants polished training videos, but supervisors may not release workers for five minutes. What is the riskiest assumption?
choices: Whether the videos look professional.
Whether supervisors will make time for workers to take the training.
Whether workers prefer tablets to printed handouts.
questions.explanation: Access controls whether training can happen at all. Video polish and format preference matter only after supervisors release workers.

questions.prompt: A founder proudly shows a long assumption list, then keeps building around the one assumption that scares her most. What is the problem?
choices: She should never list assumptions because lists create fear.
She needs more assumptions before any test is fair.
She has turned assumption work into paperwork instead of steering.
questions.explanation: The list is useful only if it changes test order. Avoiding the frightening assumption leaves the plan exposed where failure would cost most.

questions.prompt: A childcare swap organizer wants matching software, but parents hesitate to leave children with another family. How should she interpret the risk?
choices: Trust is the load-bearing assumption, so one capped trial evening should precede feature work.
Software quality is the safest first test because better matching creates trust automatically.
The idea should be abandoned because trust questions cannot be tested.
questions.explanation: Trust determines whether matching features matter. A small trial can test it directly without assuming software will solve the hardest risk.

questions.prompt: A legal automation tool finds that clients still click the paid human-review option before signing, even after praising automated clause drafting. What does that reveal about the original automation plan?
choices: Clients do not understand technology and should be educated first.
Automation should be shaped around the review value instead of replacing it blindly.
The team should automate more clauses to make human review unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Paid review preference exposes the value assumption. The tool may still work, but its design must follow the trust need clients reveal.

questions.prompt: A team can test a scary payment assumption with five real buyers now or spend two weeks improving a feature users already understand. Which is better?
choices: Improve the understood feature because it will raise confidence.
Do both only after a full investor update is ready.
Test the payment assumption because its failure would make the feature polish irrelevant.
questions.explanation: The payment assumption carries higher damage if false. Feature polish is tempting because it is controllable, but it does not steer the business risk.

reviewCards.front: A plan depends on one unproved belief that would collapse the model if false. What is a leap-of-faith assumption?
reviewCards.back: It is a belief the plan depends on before proof has arrived. If that belief is false, the rest of the work may need to change shape or stop.

reviewCards.front: How do you choose which assumption to test first?
reviewCards.back: Rank assumptions by damage if false. The first test goes to the one that could break the business or make the current plan irrelevant.

reviewCards.front: Why is an assumption list not enough?
reviewCards.back: A list can become paperwork. It matters only when it changes what the team tests first and prevents people from building around the scariest unproved belief.

reviewCards.front: A team keeps polishing safe details. What should you look for?
reviewCards.back: Look for the assumption those details avoid. The safe work may be circling the claim that would embarrass or collapse the plan if tested.

reviewCards.front: Why can testing the riskiest leap feel smaller than building features?
reviewCards.back: The test may be narrow, but it touches the load-bearing belief. A feature build can look bigger while leaving the business-breaking assumption untouched.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to rank assumptions by consequence. The skill is finding the belief your plan cannot survive without, then testing it before safer work absorbs time.

ifThenPlans.plan: If the team has an assumption list, then mark the one that would break the model and schedule that test before feature polish.
If people are debating small details, then ask which unproved belief would make those details irrelevant.
If customers praise the idea, then test the payment or commitment assumption before expanding the offer.
If a process depends on another person giving time or access, then test that release point before building the training, tool, or service around it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tomorrow, choose one active project and write five assumptions. Star the one with the highest damage if false, then define a test that touches it this week.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review whether your current work is testing the riskiest assumption or improving around it. Move one task closer to the load-bearing belief.

memorableLines.text: One belief carries the whole plan: tourists will rent winter boots instead of buying them.
memorableLines.why: It makes the abstract leap visible in the boot-rental scene.

memorableLines.text: Polish should not arrive before the floor is tested.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the chapter's warning against improving around the dangerous assumption.

memorableLines.text: A leap is not a flaw in the plan.
memorableLines.why: It reframes uncertainty as the honest place to begin testing.

chapters.title: Test
chapters.hook: One phone at the host stand can teach more than a finished waitlist app.
chapters.counterintuition: An MVP is not a cheap product, but the shortest honest path to one learning cycle. The test can be rough only if it still delivers enough value to teach.
chapters.tryThisNow: Find the smallest version of your next build that can answer the assumption. Remove every feature that does not help complete one learning cycle.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Build the smallest honest learning device that exposes the assumption, measures behavior, and prevents waste before the full product exists.

breakdown.fastRead:
Olivia's host stand phone buzzes beside the reservation book. She could spend weeks building a restaurant waitlist app. Instead, she runs the whole waitlist from one phone for two nights and watches whether diners return when text updates work.

That is the standard for a minimum viable product.

The minimum viable product is not small because small is noble. It is small because the question should not need a castle to answer it. If one phone can complete a build-measure-learn cycle, the app can wait.
breakdown.deepRead:
"Do not buy sensors yet," Jonas says while a rough video is paused on a basement fuse box. The climate startup wants hardware for home energy audits. The energy bill on the table can already support a manual checklist and a walkthrough video. The question is not whether sensors would look serious. The question is whether homeowners act on advice after seeing the walkthrough.

A rough video can be a real test.

Minimum viable product means a learning instrument, not a low-status product. It has to be honest about what it can and cannot prove. A low-fidelity screen can test whether people understand a flow. A concierge service can test whether people value a result. A manual process can test whether behavior appears before software exists. None of these are shortcuts if they complete the learning cycle.

Cheapness is not the goal. Minimum waste is the goal. A sloppy test that confuses users teaches little. A small test that exposes the right assumption teaches a lot.

The size of the build should match the size of the question.

Jonas marks one line on the energy bill before the hardware debate continues. If homeowners will not act after a manual checklist and a rough walkthrough, sensors will not rescue the audit. If they do act, the following build can focus on the part that made action easier. The minimum build earns its next size by teaching.
breakdown.fullRead:
Chloe stands at admissions beside a tray of rented headsets. The visitor-experience team wants an audio guide app with maps, routes, and clips. She has six visitors, a route card, and a stopwatch. For one afternoon, she walks the route manually and listens for where people ask for help.

The test does not look like the product. It looks like the question.

Concierge / low-fidelity / manual MVPs all carry the same burden: expose the customer decision sooner. Visitors either want route help or they do not. Patients either submit movement videos or they do not. Readers either join a book-club match or they do not. Workers either accept voice prompts in the aisle or they do not. A finished platform might hide those answers under design, onboarding, and technical details. The small test brings the assumption into view.

What is the cheapest version that still tells the truth?

Michael faces that in a remote physiotherapy service. A phone is propped against a yoga block, and therapist notes are ready for three patients. The team wants a portal. He asks the patients to text movement videos for one week before any portal exists. If they will not send videos to a therapist by text, the portal may be solving a problem that is not yet proven.

This does not excuse low standards. The test must respect the customer. It cannot trick people, hide important limits, or deliver a broken experience and call the confusion learning. The word viable still matters. The test has to create enough of the promised value that the customer's behavior means something.

Frida's book-club matching page shows the same line. The landing page gets signups, but the algorithm is premature. She opens a spreadsheet beside a stack of paperbacks and makes six matches by hand. The manual work is slow. It is also precise. It tells her whether people want the match before she automates matching.

Tomas learns it on a warehouse floor. A headset cable is coiled on the packing bench, and the logistics team is pricing devices. Before procurement, he shadows pickers in one aisle and reads manual prompts through a borrowed headset. If workers reject voice guidance in a single aisle, buying devices would only make the waste more expensive.

The point is not to stay small. The point is to earn the next size. When the test teaches, the next build can be sharper. When the test fails, the team has bought the truth before it bought the machinery.

A good MVP is not the product with features missing. It is the shortest honest path to learning.

The same standard protects customers. A thin test should never be a broken promise dressed up as learning. It should deliver the core result in a smaller way, with the limits clear enough that behavior still means something. When the customer can fairly judge the value, the team can fairly trust the lesson.

examples.title: Olivia Runs the Waitlist From One Phone

planSpec.requiredBeat: Olivia runs the whole waitlist from one phone for two nights to test return visits

The reservation book makes the test fair because diners still receive the core benefit of a faster table update.

examples.whyItMatters: Hardware can make the test look serious while hiding the behavior question. The video tests whether advice changes action before the team builds the system.

examples.title: Chloe Walks the Audio Route by Hand

examples.title: Michael Asks for Texted Movement Videos

The team wants a patient portal, but nobody knows whether people will submit movement videos. Before the software estimate is approved, Michael must decide whether to ask three patients to text videos for a week. The texted videos still deliver therapist feedback, so refusal would teach about behavior rather than software polish.

examples.whyItMatters: The portal is waste if patients will not send videos. A manual service tests the core behavior before engineering turns the assumption into infrastructure.

examples.title: Frida Makes Six Matches by Spreadsheet

planSpec.requiredBeat: Frida uses a spreadsheet to make six matches by hand after a landing-page signup

examples.scenario: It took Frida one signup weekend to stop designing the algorithm. The landing page worked well enough, and the spreadsheet sat open beside a stack of paperbacks. Before writing matching rules, she made six manual matches by hand. The postmortem showed whether readers wanted the match, not whether the algorithm was elegant. The spreadsheet keeps the matching promise small enough to test before algorithm work begins.
examples.whatToDo: Make the first six matches manually after landing-page signup. Check whether readers accept and attend before building matching logic.
examples.whyItMatters: The algorithm is premature if people will not join a matched club. The spreadsheet teaches demand before automation hides the question.

examples.title: Tomas Reads Voice Prompts in One Aisle

planSpec.stakes: device procurement may be waste before workers accept voice prompts
planSpec.requiredBeat: Tomás shadows pickers and reads prompts aloud through a headset for one aisle

examples.scenario: A headset cable is coiled on the packing bench beside a borrowed headset. Before, Tomas's logistics team priced devices for the whole warehouse. After one supervisor asks whether pickers will tolerate voice prompts, he shadows workers in one aisle and reads manual prompts aloud before any procurement order is signed. The borrowed headset tests aisle behavior while the procurement form stays unopened.
examples.whatToDo: Borrow one headset, shadow pickers, and read prompts manually in a single aisle. Decide on device procurement only after workers react to the voice flow.
examples.whyItMatters: Buying devices before testing acceptance makes waste expensive. One aisle with manual prompts exposes whether the workflow helps or irritates workers.

questions.prompt: A team calls its MVP a cheap version of the final product, then ships a confusing test that leaves customers unsure what value is being offered. In the review meeting, what did it misunderstand?
choices: An MVP should be a learning instrument that is small but still honest enough to test the assumption.
An MVP should always include every feature customers requested.
An MVP should avoid customer contact until the full product is ready.
questions.explanation: The point is learning with minimum waste, not cheapness for its own sake. A confusing test can fail to teach even if it is small.

questions.prompt: A restaurant founder wants a waitlist app, but one phone could send manual text updates for two nights. Which move best fits MVP logic?
choices: Build the app first because diners expect polished software.
Run the phone-based concierge test and measure return visits.
Skip testing because restaurants already understand waitlists.
questions.explanation: The phone test completes a learning cycle before app work. It tests whether diners value updates without the waste of a full build.

questions.prompt: A climate startup wants to buy sensors for home audits, but a rough walkthrough video could test whether homeowners act on advice. What should happen first?
choices: Buy sensors to make the advice more credible.
Wait until the audit can be fully automated.
Send the video and manual checklist to test behavior.
questions.explanation: The video tests action before hardware spend. Sensors may matter later, but they are premature if homeowners ignore advice.

questions.prompt: A museum team wants an audio guide app with maps, clips, and routes, but first needs to know whether visitors actually value route help during a real afternoon visit. Which MVP best tests route value with minimum waste?
choices: A manual route walk with rented headsets and a stopwatch.
A full app prototype with every stop included.
A survey asking visitors whether audio guides are useful.
questions.explanation: The manual route tests whether visitors want route help in the museum. The full app is costly, and a survey does not expose actual route behavior.

questions.prompt: A health team wants a portal for movement videos, but nobody knows whether patients will submit videos. What is the smallest honest test?
choices: Design the portal interface and ask patients for opinions.
Ask three patients to text videos to a therapist for one week.
Buy secure video storage before testing submissions.
questions.explanation: Texted videos test the submission behavior directly. Interface opinions and storage decisions may matter after the behavior exists.

questions.prompt: A book-club founder wants an algorithm before matching any readers, even though she has a spreadsheet, six willing members, and a shelf of paperbacks. Why might a spreadsheet be the better first build?
choices: It proves spreadsheets are better than algorithms for community products.
It removes the need to understand reader preferences.
It manually tests whether readers want and accept matches before automation hides demand.
questions.explanation: Manual matching tests the customer decision sooner. The point is not that spreadsheets are superior, but that automation should wait for proven demand.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team wants to buy voice-assist devices, but workers may reject spoken prompts. What does a borrowed-headset test reveal?
choices: Whether the workflow helps pickers before procurement makes the assumption expensive.
Whether the device vendor can deliver units quickly enough.
Whether voice technology is modern enough for logistics.
questions.explanation: The borrowed headset tests worker acceptance in the aisle. Vendor timing and technology appeal miss the assumption that controls value.

questions.prompt: A team says its rough MVP failed because customers disliked the unfinished look. The test also lacked the core value customers were promised. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: Customers can never evaluate early versions.
The team confused small with viable and did not create a fair test of the assumption.
The team should have hidden the test from customers.
questions.explanation: An MVP must be small and honest enough to test value. If the core value is absent, the result may reflect a broken test rather than the assumption.

questions.prompt: A founder can build a polished platform in three months or manually deliver the result to ten customers this week. Which is better if the main question is whether customers value the result?
choices: The platform, because polish protects the brand.
Neither, because value cannot be learned without full automation.
The manual delivery, because it exposes the customer decision sooner with less waste.
questions.explanation: Manual delivery is stronger when it tests the value assumption now. Polish and automation can wait until the team knows the result matters.

reviewCards.front: What is the real purpose of a minimum viable product?
reviewCards.back: It exists to complete one learning cycle with as little waste as possible. It is a learning instrument, not a cheap excuse for a broken product.

reviewCards.front: When is a manual MVP better than software?
reviewCards.back: It is better when manual delivery exposes the customer behavior sooner. If one person, phone, spreadsheet, or borrowed headset can test the assumption, automation can wait.

reviewCards.front: A rough MVP confuses users and hides the core value. What does viable mean in MVP?
reviewCards.back: Viable means the test creates enough of the promised value for the result to mean something. Small is useful only when the test is still honest.

reviewCards.front: A team wants to build infrastructure before testing behavior. What should you ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask what smaller device could expose the behavior first. If a rough video, concierge service, or manual workflow can answer the question, infrastructure is premature.

reviewCards.front: Why is an MVP not the final product with features missing?
reviewCards.back: Because its shape should come from the question, not from a shrunken roadmap. The right MVP may be manual, low-fidelity, or concierge if that reaches learning faster.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to build the smallest honest learning device. The skill is removing everything that does not help expose the assumption while keeping enough value for customer behavior to mean something.

ifThenPlans.plan: If the team wants a platform, then ask whether a spreadsheet, phone, or manual service can test the same customer decision first.
If procurement appears before behavior evidence, then borrow, simulate, or manually deliver one workflow before buying devices.
If the full service seems large, then deliver the core result to a few customers by hand and measure whether they value it.
If an MVP feels cheap or confusing, then restore the minimum value needed for a fair test and cut only the parts unrelated to learning.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tomorrow, take one planned build and write a manual or low-fidelity version that could answer the same assumption within a week.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Every week, inspect one build request and ask whether it is the shortest honest path to learning. Replace one overbuilt plan with a smaller test that still delivers the core value.

memorableLines.text: The minimum viable product is not small because small is noble.
memorableLines.why: It blocks the common cheapness misread of MVP.

memorableLines.text: The size of the build should match the size of the question.
memorableLines.why: It gives a practical standard for scoping tests.

memorableLines.text: The test does not look like the product.
memorableLines.why: It makes room for manual, concierge, and low-fidelity MVPs.

chapters.title: Measure
chapters.hook: A steep signup line can hide a flat week of real activation.
chapters.counterintuition: The prettiest number looks useful, but the real test is whether the metric can steer a decision, be understood, and trace back to behavior.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take one dashboard number and ask three questions: what decision can it change, who can understand it, and how would we audit its source?
chapters.keyTakeaway: Replace impressive totals with actionable, accessible, auditable measures that show whether the engine is improving from a real baseline.

breakdown.fastRead:
Megan's banking dashboard has one steep total line. Signups rose after launch. The room wants to celebrate. Then she splits users by signup week and checks the activation event against the baseline week.

The chart becomes less flattering and more useful.

Innovation accounting makes the number answerable: what decision can this metric improve, and could someone trace how it was made? A total can impress while hiding whether new users behave better. A cohort table can show whether the engine is actually tuning.
breakdown.deepRead:
"Enrollment is not completion," Henrik says while the projector shows a full enrollment bar. The education platform has more students, but refund notes are rising. He replaces the vanity chart with completion cohorts tied to the first lesson event.

A cohort line can reveal that yesterday's users behave differently from last month's, even while the total keeps rising.

Innovation accounting has three jobs. It must be actionable, so a result can change a decision. It must be accessible, so the people doing the work can understand it without a private analyst translating every meeting. It must be auditable, so the team can trace the number back to behavior rather than trusting a dashboard label.

Vanity metrics fail because they let everyone feel informed without forcing a choice. Total users, total downloads, total visits, and total signups can all be real numbers and still be weak evidence. They become useful only when connected to a baseline, cohort, or engine variable that shows improvement.

A number earns trust when it can make a team uncomfortable.

Henrik asks one student-support lead to trace the number back to a real learner. The total enrollment bar cannot answer which cohort finished lesson one, requested help, or asked for a refund. Once the team can trace the count, the next move becomes less vague: fix the first lesson, change the promise, or stop buying traffic that creates weak completions.
breakdown.fullRead:
Anke taps the lab-result icon on a patient portal screen. The hospital IT report says logins are up. The login logs are easy to praise. The lab-result event is harder and more important: did the patients who signed up actually view the result they came for?

She traces one patient cohort from signup to lab-result viewing and adds the audit trail.

This is the heart of decision-ready measurement. A metric should tell the team whether the key behavior is improving. If the engine is patient task completion, logins are only a doorway. If the engine is seller retention, first listings are only the first step. If the engine is borrowing behavior, e-card creation is not enough. The useful measure sits closer to the action the business needs.

Which number would you trust enough to pivot on?

Ryan faces that question in a recommerce warehouse. A garment rack is covered with handwritten seller tags, and listing counts look strong. First-time sellers may never return. He builds an auditable baseline for second listings, exports the seller cohort, and checks whether people list again after the first sale. The second-listing metric is less glamorous than total listings. It is also closer to whether the marketplace can keep supply alive.

Cohort analysis gives measurement timing. A baseline tells the team where it started. Cohorts tell whether newer groups behave differently from older ones. Without those two pieces, improvement can be an illusion created by volume. More people entering the top can hide weaker behavior below.

Catarina learns this in an e-card campaign. Temporary library cards stack up after the ads, and the team wants to expand spend. She measures borrowing by signup cohort first. If new cardholders do not borrow, the campaign is creating accounts, not readers. The ad spend limit stays in place until the borrow event moves.

The counterargument is that totals still matter. They do. A business eventually needs scale. But scale before learning can blur the signal. Early measurement should help decide whether to tune, pivot, or persevere. Later measurement can track whether a known engine is producing enough volume.

Luke sees the same issue in fleet maintenance. A tablet is mounted beside the service bay, and download counts impress the transport company. Before rollout, he asks mechanics to verify the metric trail from install to completed inspection. The install log, inspection event, and mechanic initials form a chain someone can audit. Without that chain, downloads can look like adoption while the workflow stays unused.

The best number is rarely the biggest number. It is the one that tells the team what to do next.

That is why accessible measurement matters as much as accuracy. If only one analyst can explain the number, the team cannot use it in time. If the working team can see the behavior behind the count, they can challenge it, trust it, and act before the next review turns into theater.

examples.title: Megan Splits the Signup Line

planSpec.stakes: total signups could hide whether new users activate better
planSpec.requiredBeat: Megan splits users by signup week before accepting the launch metric

examples.scenario: At 10:15 a.m. Monday, Megan studies a dashboard with one steep total line and a baseline week circled in pencil. The launch metric says signups are up. The cohort table is still hidden, and the activation event may not have moved. Before the analytics review, she must choose between accepting the total and splitting users by signup week. The baseline week gives Megan a starting point before the team claims the dashboard improved.
examples.whatToDo: Split the signup total into cohorts and compare activation against the baseline week. Let activation behavior decide whether onboarding improved.
examples.whyItMatters: Total signups can rise while new users fail to activate. Cohorts make the number decision-ready by showing whether the engine changed.

examples.title: Henrik Replaces the Enrollment Bar

planSpec.stakes: enrollment growth may conceal falling completion
planSpec.requiredBeat: Henrik replaces the vanity chart with cohort completion curves

examples.scenario: "That bar tells us who arrived, not who learned," Henrik says as the projector shows a full enrollment bar. Refund notes are stacked beside the laptop, and the first lesson event is tagged in the data. The platform team has to choose between celebrating enrollment growth and replacing the vanity chart with cohort completion curves. The first-lesson cohort shows Henrik whether enrollment turned into learning rather than refunds.
examples.whatToDo: Chart completion cohorts from the first lesson event and compare them with refund notes. Use completion, not enrollment, to decide what needs tuning.
examples.whyItMatters: Enrollment can conceal a weakening course experience. Completion cohorts reveal whether newer students are actually moving through the product.

examples.title: Anke Follows the Lab-Result Event

planSpec.stakes: login totals may not show whether patients complete the intended task
planSpec.requiredBeat: Anke traces one patient cohort from signup to lab-result viewing

examples.scenario: The lab-result icon glows on the patient portal screen while Anke compares login logs with an audit trail. The hospital IT group wants to report higher usage. She has a decision to make before the slide is sent: show login totals, or trace one patient cohort from signup to the lab-result event they actually needed. The lab-result event ties the patient portal to the task patients actually came to complete.
examples.whatToDo: Trace the cohort from signup to lab-result viewing and keep the audit trail visible. Report task completion instead of login totals alone.
examples.whyItMatters: A login is a doorway, not the intended task. Lab-result viewing shows whether patients completed the behavior the portal exists to support.

examples.title: Ryan Builds a Second-Listing Baseline

planSpec.stakes: listing counts may rise while first-time sellers never return
planSpec.requiredBeat: Ryan builds an auditable baseline for second listings

examples.scenario: You are beside Ryan in a recommerce warehouse, where a garment rack carries handwritten seller tags and the listing count looks healthy. The seller cohort export is ready, but the second-listing metric is not in the review. Before the funding update, Ryan needs to decide whether to report total listings or build an auditable baseline for sellers who list again. The seller cohort keeps Ryan from mistaking first listings for a marketplace with returning supply.
examples.whatToDo: Export the seller cohort and define the second-listing baseline. Use repeat listings to decide whether seller supply is improving.
examples.whyItMatters: Listing counts can rise while first-time sellers disappear. A second-listing metric makes retention visible and traceable.

examples.title: Catarina Checks Borrowing Before More Ads

planSpec.stakes: card creation totals may not prove borrowing behavior
planSpec.requiredBeat: Catarina measures borrowing by signup cohort before expanding ads

examples.scenario: At 6:05 p.m. in the public library workroom, Catarina sorts a stack of temporary e-card printouts after one ad cycle. As digital-access lead, she sees that accounts are up and the ad spend limit is nearly raised. In the postmortem, she groups new cards by signup week and checks borrowing behavior before approving another campaign. The borrowing event decides whether the ad campaign created readers or only accounts.
examples.whatToDo: Measure borrowing by signup cohort before expanding ads. Keep the spend limit until card creation turns into borrowing behavior.
examples.whyItMatters: Card totals prove account creation, not reading activity. Borrowing by cohort shows whether the campaign creates library use.

examples.title: Luke Verifies the Inspection Trail

planSpec.stakes: download counts may impress while mechanics ignore the workflow
planSpec.requiredBeat: Luke asks mechanics to verify the metric trail from install to completed inspection

examples.scenario: A tablet is mounted beside the service bay with the install log open. Before, Luke's transport company celebrated download counts for the maintenance app. After mechanics initial the inspection event and trace the workflow from install to completed inspection, he sees which downloads became real work and which never left the screen. The mechanic initials make the install metric auditable at the service bay, not just on a dashboard.
examples.whatToDo: Ask mechanics to verify the trail from install to inspection completion. Count completed inspections with initials, not app downloads alone.
examples.whyItMatters: Downloads can impress while the workflow is ignored. A verified inspection trail makes adoption auditable by the people doing the work.

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows total users rising, but the team cannot tell whether newer users activate more often. What kind of measurement is missing?
choices: A cohort or baseline view that links the number to activation behavior.
A larger chart that makes the growth easier to present.
A single monthly total that everyone can remember.
questions.explanation: The team needs a metric that can steer activation decisions. Larger or simpler totals may be accessible, but they still hide behavior by cohort.

questions.prompt: An education platform has enrollment growth and falling completion. Which measure should guide the next product decision?
choices: Total enrollments because they show demand.
Completion cohorts tied to the first lesson event.
Social comments from students who liked the course page.
questions.explanation: Completion cohorts show whether the course experience is improving. Enrollments and comments are weaker if the decision concerns learning completion.

questions.prompt: A hospital portal report celebrates logins, but patients mainly need to view lab results. Which metric is more actionable?
choices: The number of portal logins per month.
The number of patients who saw the portal home screen.
The share of a signup cohort that reaches the lab-result event.
questions.explanation: Lab-result viewing measures the intended task. Login counts are real but too far from the patient behavior the portal is meant to improve.

questions.prompt: A recommerce marketplace has more listings, but first-time sellers may never return. Which metric best tests the supply engine?
choices: A second-listing rate by seller cohort.
The total number of listing photos uploaded.
The number of sellers who opened the listing page.
questions.explanation: Second-listing rate shows whether seller behavior repeats. Photos and page opens can rise without proving sellers return.

questions.prompt: A public library campaign creates many e-cards after a week of ads, and the team wants to increase ad spend before the next board report. The stacks of new cards look impressive, but no one has checked reading behavior. What should it measure first?
choices: The visual appeal of the e-card sign-up page.
Borrowing behavior by signup cohort.
The number of staff who shared the campaign link.
questions.explanation: Borrowing by cohort shows whether account creation turns into library use. Page appeal and staff sharing are not the behavior the spend should buy.

questions.prompt: A maintenance app has a thousand downloads, but mechanics may not complete inspections through it. Why is download count a vanity metric here?
choices: It is too easy for executives to understand.
It cannot be stored in an auditable database.
It does not show whether the workflow reached the inspection event.
questions.explanation: The decision concerns workflow adoption, so completed inspections matter. A number can be understandable and auditable while still measuring the wrong thing.

questions.prompt: A team says a metric is actionable, accessible, and auditable during a dashboard review. The product manager asks for an example that can change a decision, be understood by the team, and be traced back to user behavior. Which example best fits all three?
choices: A weekly cohort table showing activation, readable by the product team, with source events listed.
A proprietary health score only the analytics lead can explain.
A total signup count copied from a slide without event definitions.
questions.explanation: The cohort table can change decisions, be understood, and be traced. The health score lacks accessibility, and the slide total lacks auditability.

questions.prompt: A product lead wants to pivot after seeing a bad total revenue month, but cohort retention is improving. What should the team analyze before deciding?
choices: Whether revenue should be ignored until the product is mature.
Whether the decision should use engine-specific metrics rather than one aggregate total.
Whether the pivot would sound persuasive to investors.
questions.explanation: Pivot decisions need evidence tied to the engine being tuned. Aggregate revenue may matter, but it can hide improving retention behavior.

questions.prompt: A team can present a beautiful growth dashboard or a rough cohort table that reveals activation is weaker in newer users. Which should guide the meeting?
choices: The beautiful dashboard because leaders need confidence.
Neither, because early teams should avoid numbers.
The rough cohort table because it is closer to the decision the team must make.
questions.explanation: The cohort table is less flattering but more decision-ready. Confidence and number avoidance both dodge the measurement job.

reviewCards.front: What makes a metric actionable?
reviewCards.back: It can change a real decision. If no one can say what they would do differently when the number moves, the metric is probably decorative.

reviewCards.front: Why are totals often dangerous in startup measurement?
reviewCards.back: Totals can rise while newer users behave worse. Cohorts and baselines show whether the engine is improving instead of hiding behavior under volume.

reviewCards.front: What does auditable mean for a metric?
reviewCards.back: Someone can trace the number back to real events or behavior. It is not just a label on a dashboard that everyone has to trust.

reviewCards.front: A team wants to pivot from one bad month. What should you check first?
reviewCards.back: Check the engine-specific measures and cohort behavior. A pivot-or-persevere decision needs stronger evidence than one aggregate total.

reviewCards.front: How does innovation accounting differ from ordinary reporting?
reviewCards.back: It is built to steer uncertainty. The numbers are chosen because they reveal learning quality, baseline movement, and engine tuning, not because they look impressive.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to turn numbers into decisions. The skill is replacing attractive totals with measures that are actionable, accessible, auditable, and tied to the engine being tuned.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a metric is a total, then split it by cohort or baseline before using it to claim progress.
If a number is praised, then ask what decision it can change and whether the team can trace its source events.
If signups are up, then check whether activation, retention, referral, or payment improved in the cohort that matters.
If adoption is reported as downloads or logins, then follow the metric trail to the completed workflow event.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tomorrow, choose one dashboard metric and rewrite it as an actionable, accessible, auditable measure with a baseline or cohort view.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, pick one celebrated number and ask whether it would support a pivot-or-persevere decision. If not, replace it with a measure closer to the engine.

memorableLines.text: The chart becomes less flattering and more useful.
memorableLines.why: It captures the tradeoff between vanity and decision-ready measurement.

memorableLines.text: A number earns trust when it can make a team uncomfortable.
memorableLines.why: It makes good metrics feel consequential rather than decorative.

memorableLines.text: The best number is rarely the biggest number.
memorableLines.why: It gives readers a compact warning against impressive totals.

chapters.title: Pivot (or Persevere)
chapters.hook: The fridge magnet holds two charts, and one of them is asking the founder to stop pretending.
chapters.counterintuition: Staying the course can backfire when it protects a weak bet. A pivot is disciplined only when it names a sharper hypothesis for the next test.
chapters.tryThisNow: Choose one struggling project and write: persevere if this metric improves by X, pivot if it does not. Name the new hypothesis before changing anything.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Use validated learning to choose: persevere when evidence improves, pivot when a specific new hypothesis deserves the next test.

breakdown.fastRead:
Kasia stands in the meal-kit office with a fridge magnet holding two retention charts. Families were the original plan. Single-person users are the group still returning. The pivot agenda is full of opinions until she moves the meeting to the segment chart.

The meeting is not about whether the old idea feels lovable. It is about whether the evidence has earned another cycle.

A pivot is a structured course correction. It keeps the discipline of testing but changes the hypothesis. Persevering is also a decision. It needs evidence, not loyalty.
breakdown.deepRead:
"We have cash for one semester, but not room for six more guesses," Julien says beside a whiteboard of crossed-out tutoring models. The cash balance looks fine. The hypothesis list does not. Only two meaningful changes remain before students stop trusting the project.

Runway is not just money when the last useful test is gone.

A team can persevere when the evidence is improving and the current hypothesis still deserves another test. It can pivot when the evidence shows the current hypothesis is weak but the learning points toward a better one. The key is specificity. A pivot should name what changes: customer segment, channel, pricing, product form, growth mechanism, or value promise. Without that new hypothesis, the team is only wandering with a better vocabulary.

Validated learning protects the decision from mood. Attachment says, we have come too far. Panic says, change everything. Evidence asks what has been learned and what should be tested next.

The choice should feel sober, not dramatic.

Julien adds one column to the whiteboard before the team votes. Each possible change must name the new hypothesis, the evidence that would support it, and the decision it would unlock. The exercise slows the room down in the useful way. A pivot without that column is just movement. Persevering without it is just attachment with a longer calendar.
breakdown.fullRead:
Paula looks at the nurse station monitor showing missed portal bookings. Staff praise the clinic scheduling tool because it saves them steps. Appointment data shows patients are not adopting it. She writes a segment note: maybe the first users should be caregivers booking for older parents, not patients booking for themselves.

That is a Pivot or persevere decision when the next move becomes a testable hypothesis.

The course correction has to preserve learning. If Paula simply redesigns everything because adoption is weak, the team loses the thread. If she keeps pushing the same patient portal because staff like it, she protects the old idea from evidence. The disciplined move is narrower: define a customer-segment pivot and run the next test against caregiver bookings.

What evidence would make staying the wiser choice?

Matthew faces the opposite pressure at a winter fair. Handmade mugs fill the table, and sellers love the artisan marketplace. The seller survey is warm. Buyer conversion after the price test is poor. He wants to persevere because the sellers are loyal and the story feels good. Before doing that, he compares buyer conversion to seller enthusiasm. If buyers resist the price, seller love alone cannot carry the market.

Runway measured in meaningful pivots changes the math: a team can have months of cash and almost no runway if it has burned through the chances to learn differently. Runway is learning capacity. Money matters because it buys cycles, but a cycle only counts when it tests a meaningful new hypothesis. Spending another month on the same weak bet may consume more runway than the bank account suggests.

Lea's compliance app team learns this after a failed outreach list. Direct sales to enterprise buyers barely moved. Partner call notes suggest compliance consultants may carry trust into the room. In the postmortem, she frames a channel pivot as a new hypothesis, not desperation: perhaps partners, not direct outreach, are the path to adoption. The new channel test will prove or weaken that claim.

There is a cost to pivoting too early. Every hard week can make a new direction feel clean. But changing before the evidence has had time to mature turns strategy into restlessness. The decision needs a threshold. What result would justify another cycle? What result would make the new hypothesis more responsible than the old one?

Hugo sees the same threshold in compost pickup. A route map is taped to a bin lid, and the lease deadline for another truck is close. Before, the team expanded routes as if persistence were virtue. After building a route density map and calling building managers, he sees that apartment density may matter more than neighborhood enthusiasm. The next decision is whether to pivot customer segment before signing the lease.

To pivot well is to keep faith with the evidence, not with the original plan. To persevere well is to keep testing because the evidence still deserves it, not because quitting would hurt.

examples.title: Kasia Moves the Pivot Meeting to Retention

planSpec.stakes: attachment to the original family plan may outlast evidence from single-person users
planSpec.requiredBeat: Kasia moves the pivot meeting from opinions to the retention evidence by segment

examples.scenario: At 2:30 p.m. Wednesday, Kasia stands by a fridge magnet holding two retention charts and a runway note. The pivot agenda still says family plan review, but the segment chart shows single-person users returning more often. Before the meeting drifts into opinions, Kasia must choose whether to defend the original family idea or move the room to retention evidence. The retention chart is the only object allowed to decide the next cycle.
examples.whatToDo: Put the segment chart at the center of the meeting. Decide whether to persevere with families or test a single-person hypothesis based on retention evidence.
examples.whyItMatters: Attachment to the original customer can outlast the data. Segment retention turns the pivot decision into evidence, not a loyalty test.

examples.title: Julien Counts Meaningful Pivots

planSpec.stakes: cash may last but only two hypothesis changes remain
planSpec.requiredBeat: Julien counts remaining meaningful pivots before another semester build

examples.scenario: "The cash balance says yes, but the semester calendar says no," Julien says beside a whiteboard with crossed-out business models. The hypothesis list has only two credible changes left. Another build is about to start. The student founders must choose between spending the semester on the current model and counting how many meaningful pivots remain. The whiteboard forces the founders to count learning chances, not just bank weeks.
examples.whatToDo: Count the remaining hypothesis changes before approving another build. Treat runway as learning capacity, not only the cash balance in the account.
examples.whyItMatters: The team can have money and still run out of useful ways to learn. Counting meaningful pivots keeps another semester from becoming repetition.

examples.title: Paula Writes a Caregiver Segment Note

planSpec.stakes: staff praise may mask weak patient adoption
planSpec.requiredBeat: Paula proposes a customer-segment pivot tied to appointment data

examples.scenario: The nurse station monitor shows missed portal bookings while Paula reads appointment data under the night shift lights. Staff praise is strong, but patient adoption is weak. She has a decision to make before the next sprint: keep improving the same patient flow or write a new hypothesis that tests caregivers as the first customer segment. The note on the monitor must become a customer-segment test, not another staff-request ticket.
examples.whatToDo: Frame the customer-segment pivot as a testable hypothesis. Use appointment data to design a caregiver booking experiment instead of treating staff praise as enough.
examples.whyItMatters: Staff value and patient adoption are different signals. Paula's pivot preserves learning by changing the segment rather than changing everything at once.

examples.title: Matthew Compares Buyers With Sellers

planSpec.stakes: seller loyalty may keep the founder from seeing buyer resistance
planSpec.requiredBeat: Matthew compares buyer conversion to seller enthusiasm before persevering

examples.scenario: You are beside Matthew at a winter fair, where handmade mugs cover the table and the seller survey glows with praise. The price test tells a colder story: buyer conversion is low. Before he books another seller push, Matthew needs to decide whether seller enthusiasm is enough to persevere or whether buyer resistance demands a pricing pivot. The cash box on the table makes the choice concrete because buyer behavior, not seller warmth, decides the next market bet.
examples.whatToDo: Compare buyer conversion with seller enthusiasm before committing. Persevere only if buyer evidence improves, or define the pricing hypothesis to test next.
examples.whyItMatters: A marketplace needs both sides. Seller loyalty can hide buyer resistance, and buyer behavior decides whether the current pricing idea deserves another cycle.

examples.title: Lea Turns Partner Interest Into a Channel Hypothesis

planSpec.stakes: direct sales effort may fail while partners could carry trust
planSpec.requiredBeat: Lea frames channel pivot as a new hypothesis rather than desperation

examples.scenario: It took Lea a failed outreach list to stop calling every channel change desperation. A partner brochure sits beside the direct sales report, and partner call notes show consultants already carry trust with buyers. In the postmortem, she frames the channel pivot as a new hypothesis: partner-led demos may open doors direct emails cannot. The new channel test gets a date and a success threshold before anyone calls the pivot strategic.
examples.whatToDo: Write the partner channel as a hypothesis and run a limited new channel test. Do not call it a pivot unless the next experiment can prove or weaken it.
examples.whyItMatters: A pivot is not flailing when it follows learning. Lea keeps the team disciplined by turning channel change into a testable course correction.

examples.title: Hugo Checks Density Before the Truck Lease

planSpec.stakes: route expansion may be persistence when apartment density evidence points elsewhere
planSpec.requiredBeat: Hugo chooses whether to pivot customer segment before the next truck lease

examples.scenario: A route map is taped to Hugo's compost bin lid, and the lease deadline for a second truck is circled. Before, Hugo expanded blocks because neighbors sounded supportive. After building a route density map and calling building managers, he sees apartment clusters may carry the service. The next choice is segment pivot or truck lease. The density map has to answer the lease question before another truck turns a guess into fixed cost.
